en: The Commentary on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, composed by the Śramaṇa Jizang:

The Dharma-body is profound and tranquil, its lifespan being neither long nor short; the Perfected Person transcends all discursive thought, yet there is nothing that does not respond to their resonance. Great!

These were taught through provisional skillful means to respond to the capacities of sentient beings: thus, the four Buddhas appeared in the chamber to proclaim the principle of eternal abiding, and the Bodhisattvas responded to the dream to expound the methods of repentance. Because these two virtues are combined, they encompass all practices; as a result, one ascends to spiritual awakening, with a lifespan equal to empty space.

Therefore, the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages cultivate this principle, and the Four Heavenly Kings praise and protect the merit of this sutra. By relying on this sutra for exposition, obstacles and difficulties are dispelled; by entrusting oneself to the Dharma and making vows, blessings and joy follow one's heart. Thus, this sutra takes the Middle Way of the True Dharma as its essence and the Three Points and Four Virtues as its core doctrine.

If one were to preserve the authentic Indic pronunciation in its entirety, it should be called *buddhaprajñāpāramitāsūtra*. *Buddha* means "the Awakened One," and *prajñā* means "wisdom," though both [prefixes] have been omitted here. *Pāramitā* means "perfection," and *sūtra* means "discourse. Thus, it is the discourse on the perfection of wisdom of the Awakened One. Furthermore, because this treatise is vast, it is called "Great" (*mahā-*) to distinguish it from other versions. It is also called "Heart" (*hṛdaya*) because it extracts the essential meaning from within the extensive text. It is also called "Essential Meaning" (*artha*) because it reveals the profound significance of the Dharma. It is also called "Profound" (*gambhīra*) because its meaning is difficult to fathom. It is also called "Difficult to Practice" (*duṣkara*) because it is hard to enter. It is also called "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) because there is nothing superior to it. It is also called "Supreme" (*parama*) because it is the most excellent among all dharmas. It is also called "Peerless" (*asama*) because there is no equal to it. It is also called "Incomparable" (*apratima*) because there is nothing with which it can be compared. It is also called "Unequaled" (*asamasama*) because there is no dharma that can be equated with it. It is also called "The Mother of All Buddhas" (*sarvabuddhamātṛkā*) because it gives birth to all Tathāgatas. It is also called "The Source of All Dharmas" (*sarvadharmanidāna*) because it is the origin of all phenomena. It is also called "The Treasury of All Jewels" (*sarvaratnakośa*) because it contains all the jewels of the Dharma. It is also called "The Lamp Illuminating All Darkness" (*sarvatamondhakāravidhamanapradīpa*) because it dispels all the darkness of ignorance. It is also called "The Medicine Healing All Sicknesses" (*sarvaglānyapraśamanabhaiṣajya*) because it cures all the ailments of afflictions. It is also called "The Armor for Protecting All Beings" (*sarvasattvarakṣāsaṃnāha*) because it protects all sentient beings. It is also called "The Bridge for Crossing Over All Worlds" (*sarvalokottaraṇasetu*) because it enables the crossing over of the ocean of saṃsāra. It is also called "The Ship Carrying All to the Other Shore" (*sarvapārasaṃtāraṇanau*) because it carries all sentient beings across to the shore of nirvāṇa. It is also called "The King of All Dharmas" (*sarvadharmarāja*) because it reigns supreme over all dharmas. It is also called "The Sovereign of All Dharmas" (*sarvadharmeśvara*) because it has mastery over all dharmas. It is also called "The Lord of All Dharmas" (*sarvadharmādhipati*) because it governs all dharmas. It is also called "The Master of All Dharmas" (*sarvadharmasvāmī*) because it is the master of all dharmas. It is also called "The Unobstructed Wisdom" (*asaṅgaprajñā*) because its wisdom is free from all obstructions. It is also called "The Unimpeded Wisdom" (*apratihatajñāna*) because its knowledge is unimpeded regarding all things. It is also called "The Mirror of All Dharmas" (*sarvadharmādarśa*) because it reflects all dharmas without distortion. It is also called "The Sun Illuminating All Worlds" (*sarvalokāvabhāsaprabhākarasūrya*) because it shines light upon all worlds. It is also called "The Moon Cooling All Beings" (*sarvasattvaśītīkaraṇacandramaṇḍala*) because it cools the fever of the afflictions of all sentient beings. It is also called "The Thunderbolt Shattering All Evil Maras" (*sarvamāraparapravādinirdalanavajra*) because it shatters all evil Māras and externalists. It is also called "The Wheel-Turning King of the Dharma" (*dharmacakravartin*) because it turns the wheel of the sublime Dharma. It is also called "The Lion's Roar of the Buddha" (*buddhasiṃhanāda*) because it utters the lion’s roar of fearlessness. It is also called "The Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*) because it is the vehicle that carries the great bodhisattvas. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas" (*bodhisattvayāna*) because it is the vehicle traversed by all bodhisattvas. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Tathāgatas" (*tathāgatayāna*) because it is the vehicle that leads to the state of a Tathāgata. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Buddhas" (*buddhayāna*) because it is the vehicle that results in the attainment of Buddhahood. It is also called "The Vehicle of Liberation" (*vimuktyāna*) because it leads to liberation from all bonds. It is also called "The Vehicle of Nirvāṇa" (*nirvāṇayāna*) because it leads to the city of nirvāṇa. It is also called "The Vehicle of Peace" (*śāntiyāna*) because it brings peace to all sentient beings. It is also called "The Vehicle of Bliss" (*sukhayāna*) because it bestows the bliss of the Dharma upon all sentient beings. It is also called "The Vehicle of Emptiness" (*śūnyatāyāna*) because it reveals the gate of emptiness. It is also called "The Vehicle of Signlessness" (*animittayāna*) because it reveals the gate of signlessness. It is also called "The Vehicle of Wishlessness" (*apraṇihitayāna*) because it reveals the gate of wishlessness. It is also called "The Vehicle of Non-arising" (*anutpādāyāna*) because it reveals the gate of non-arising. It is also called "The Vehicle of Non-extinction" (*anirodhāyāna*) because it reveals the gate of non-extinction. It is also called "The Vehicle of Non-duality" (*advayayāna*) because it reveals the gate of non-duality. It is also called "The Vehicle of Non-distinction" (*anānātvayāna*) because it reveals the gate of non-distinction. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Single Path" (*ekamārgayāna*) because it reveals the single path of the Dharma. It is also called "The Vehicle of the True Dharma" (*saddharmayāna*) because it reveals the true Dharma. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Ultimate Truth" (*paramārthayāna*) because it reveals the ultimate truth. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Profound Meaning" (*gambhīrārthayāna*) because it reveals the profound meaning. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Inconceivable" (*acintyayāna*) because it reveals the inconceivable. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Inexpressible" (*anabhilāpyayāna*) because it reveals the inexpressible. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Ungraspable" (*agrāhyayāna*) because it reveals the ungraspable. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Unobtainable" (*anupalabhyayāna*) because it reveals the unobtainable. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛtayāna*) because it reveals the unconditioned. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Unborn" (*ajānayāna*) because it reveals the unborn. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Unoriginated" (*anutpannayāna*) because it reveals the unoriginated. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Unceased" (*aniruddhayāna*) because it reveals the unceased. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Tranquil" (*śāntayāna*) because it reveals the tranquil. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Cooled" (*śītībhūtayāna*) because it reveals the cooled. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Exhausted" (*kṣīṇayāna*) because it reveals the exhausted. It is also called "The Vehicle of the Vanished" (*vigatayāna*) because it reveals the vanished.
*Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is translated here as "Golden Light.
*Sūtra* contains five meanings, which are here represented by the term "jīng" (sūtra).
"Sūtra" (jing) means "instruction in the Dharma" and "instruction in the eternal," as well as "the path traversed.
Hence it is called the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is subsumed within the ultimate Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-piṭaka and is categorized among the teachings of the sudden (sudden teaching).
Discussing its ultimate tenet, it manifests three sets of three dharmas:
first, it manifests the three bodies as the fruit of Buddhahood; second, it manifests the three virtues of nirvāṇa; and third, it manifests the three kinds of Buddha-nature.

To represent the three bodies: the gold substance, being true and real, is a metaphor for the Dharma-body Buddha; the light and function, being able to illuminate, are a metaphor for the Response-body Buddha; and the brilliance, being able to benefit all universally, is like the Transformation-body Buddha.

Regarding the second analogy for the three virtues: the four meanings of the substance of gold are used to illustrate the four virtues of the Dharmakāya. Its color remaining unchanged is like *nitya* (permanence); its substance being unstained is like *śubha* (purity); its transformation being unimpeded is like *ātman* (self); and its making people wealthy and noble is like *sukha* (bliss).
Next, "light" (ābhā) has two meanings:
the ability to illuminate and the ability to remove, as in the case of *prajñā*.
Next, "clarity" (prakāśa) has two meanings:
It is without darkness and as vast and far-reaching as liberation, entirely free from all afflictions.
Regarding the third [aspect], which manifests the three kinds of Buddha-nature: the golden essence is inherently present, like the correct cause (正因) prior to the Path;
the luminous function begins to manifest, like the revealing cause (了因) within the Path.
Brightness is the absence of darkness, just as the path leads to the subsequent attainment of the fruit.
By using the three meanings of gold and so forth as metaphors for the three sets of three dharmas, it is called the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
The introduction is explained as usual.
These three types and three meanings are fully contained within the seven fascicles.
Within these four fascicles, there is a general division into three sections:
First, the "Introductory Chapter" constitutes the introductory section;
second, from the "Chapter on Lifespan" through the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body," constitutes the main explanatory section.
Third, the chapter "Praising the Buddha" is the section on the dissemination [of the teaching].
There are two reasons for this threefold division:
first, it is explained from the perspective of the teacher who converts others.
If there were no introductory discourse, sentient beings would not give rise to faith.
If one were to speak abruptly without faith, sentient beings would not accept it; consequently, the Tathāgata would incur the fault of empty speech. Therefore, there is an introductory discourse.
If there were sentient beings with faith yet the Tathāgata did not preach for them, he would incur the fault of missing the opportune moment; therefore, there is the "Correct Teaching.
Once the Correct Teaching is revealed, if it were not circulated, the Tathāgata would incur the fault of lacking great compassion; therefore, there is the teaching on "Circulation."
Second, regarding the explanation according to those to be converted: since the faith of sentient beings entering the Path is primary, there is the introductory teaching;
because understanding arises based on faith, there is the main teaching;
and because practice is initiated based on understanding, there is the dissemination.
The introduction consists of two parts:
"Thus have I heard" is the sequence for attesting to faith;
"At one time," and so forth, is the sequence for the occasion of the teaching.
The analysis of the two prefaces is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*.
Within the introductory section on the occasion of the teaching (*nidāna*), there are two parts:
the three phrases beginning with "time" constitute the general introduction; [the remainder constitutes the specific introduction].
The passage beginning with "At that time, the Tathāgata" constitutes the specific introduction (*prastāvanā*).
Since the formal exposition of the various chapters below is collectively a dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is termed "general";
because it serves as a dependent origination for each specific section, it is termed "specific."
Regarding why "common hearing" (*sahāvaśravaṇa*) should be included among the factors that initiate [the teaching] but is not established as such, there are three reasons:

first, the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) was spoken by four Buddhas and was spoken within the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa; it was not heard in common with the twelve hundred [monks] and others.
Second, the "Chapter on Repentance" was seen and heard by Śraddhālakṣaṇa in a dream; it was not heard in common by the twelve hundred [disciples] and others.
Third, in the subsequent "Chapter on Praising the Buddha," the great beings from other lands went to other lands to praise the Buddha; they were not co-residents with the twelve hundred and others.
Because these three meanings exist, it is not appropriate to establish a group of co-listeners.
This implies that the preaching of this sutra occurs during four periods and in three locations.
As for the three locations, they are the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa, Vulture Peak, and another land; these are the three.
The "four times" refers to two days and one night, as well as the time when [the Buddha] is praised in other directions.
Gṛdhrakūṭa and Śrāvastī are explained as usual.
The introductory section on the specific arousal of the teaching differs from the introductions of other sūtras; it takes the secret empowerment of the three mysteries as its introduction.
The "three secrets" refer to the secrets of body, speech, and mind.
When one wishes to expound this sutra, being physically present on Vulture Peak to manifest the extraordinary excellence of this sutra constitutes the secret of the body.
Contemplating the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the protection of the four Buddhas, as well as the practices of repentance and so forth, constitutes the secret of the mind.
Furthermore, the intention to expound these profound teachings constitutes the secret of speech (*vākkarma-guhya*).

Because the faithful one (*śraddhā-lakṣaṇa*) receives the inconceivable empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of these three secrets, the doubt of the faithful one evokes the Buddhas of the four directions to proclaim the fruit of the lifespan.

Furthermore, because of these three mysteries, the signs of faith induced dreams in which the Dharma of repentance and other teachings were expounded; the Four Heavenly Kings and others made vows to propagate the sutra, even to the point of preaching the "Chapter on Sacrificing the Body. Therefore, it is said that the three mysteries constitute the introductory sequence of the arousal.
Regarding the introductory section composed separately, there are two parts:
first, the nineteen verses that serve as the introduction to the main exposition;
second, the nine and a half verses beginning with "What I have now spoken," which serve as the introduction for the propagation of the teaching.
Regarding the first part, there are two sections:
first, the eight lines of verse serve as a preface for the four chapters beginning with the "Life Span" chapter;

second, the eleven lines of verse beginning with "Those with impaired faculties" serve as a preface for the twelve chapters on the power and function beginning with the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings."
Furthermore, regarding the first section, there are two parts:
first, the five lines of verse serve as a preface to the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*);
second, the three lines of verse beginning with "I shall now speak" serve as a preface to the three chapters starting from the "Chapter on Repentance" (*Deśanā-parivarta*).
Regarding the phrase "at that time," there are three occasions:
first, when the Tathāgata intends to preach the Dharma; second, when the assembly desires to listen; and third, when the minds of the great multitude are free from pride or disparagement.
Regarding the term "Tathāgata," there are three types of Tathāgatas:
first, the Dharma-body; second, the Response-body; and third, the Transformation-body.
As for the Dharma-body Tathāgata: that which is unchanging prior to the Path is called "Thus" (tathā), and that which manifests subsequent to the Path is called "Come" (āgata).

As for the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata: he "comes as suchness" (tathā) by riding upon the path of reality; he "comes" (āgata) because he has attained perfect enlightenment. As for the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata:

his "transformation body" (nirmāṇa) and "transformed person" (puruṣa) do not miss the proper time nor wait for a specific time, thus they are "as suchness" (tathā); they proceed toward the fruit through the eight phases, thus they "come" (āgata).

What is now called the Tathāgata refers precisely to the Saṃbhogakāya and the Nirmāṇakāya; it clarifies that the Saṃbhogakāya illuminates the eternal bliss and other attributes of the Dharmakāya, while the Nirmāṇakāya intends to expound them.
Regarding "wandering in the immeasurable": the essence of the Dharma-body has no distinctions of self or other, nor any limits, and is therefore called "immeasurable.
Because the power of illumination of the wisdom of the Response-body involves movement, it is called "wandering."
Regarding the phrase "the profound nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*): "phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to the *dharmakāya*, and "nature" (*tā*) refers to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because this intrinsic nature is reality, it is called the "nature of phenomena.
This nature of phenomena is profound and difficult to fathom; therefore, it is called "profound" (*gambhīra*).
The Buddhas of the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) are able to exhaustively practice these deeds; therefore, it is called "the sphere of action of the Buddhas.
Because they have transcended all stages of training, it is called "beyond all bodhisattvas."
Because there is no longer any distinction between object and wisdom, and the two hindrances are forever exhausted, it is said that "the sphere of practice is pure.

As for the statement, "This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the king of all sūtras," this scripture is named thus because it teaches the eternal abiding of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and also manifests the threefold sets of three meanings; therefore, this title is established.
It is called a "king" because it surpasses the Hīnayāna.
From the words "If there are those who hear it" onwards, the text next praises the utility of the sūtra.
"If there are those who hear it" gives rise to the wisdom born of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā).
"Then one is able to contemplate" gives rise to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);
"the unsurpassed, subtle, and profoundly deep meaning" gives rise to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
From the passage "such a sūtra" onwards, it clarifies the person who is capable of expounding [it].
The mention of the Buddhas of the four directions serves to manifest that the paths of all Buddhas are identical.
The number is specified as four solely to represent the four virtues; thus, it is neither five nor six.
The immovable one in the east symbolizes the virtue of permanence (*nityatā*).
The Jewel-Aspect (*Ratnaketu*) in the south—the Jewel-Aspect being the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) that possesses sovereign power—symbolizes the virtue of self (*ātman*).
The Western Land of Immeasurable Life is the Land of Peace and Bliss, which symbolizes the virtue of bliss.
The Northern Land of Sublime Sound possesses a voice free from defilement and turbidity, which symbolizes the virtue of purity.
From the title of the *Dharmatā-sūtra* above, we see its function: it is able to expound such dharmas as these, all of which are the spheres traversed by the Tathāgata’s intentional resolve.
The section beginning with "I shall now speak" constitutes the second introduction.
Within this, there are three parts:
the first half-verse indicates the subject, the next two verses provide the explanation, and the final half-verse offers the conclusion.
The initial mention of "repentance" (chanhui) refers to the "Chapter on Repentance."
"Equal dharmas" refers to the latter two categories.

Alternatively, within the five dharmas for repentance, one may specifically perform repentance; "equal dharmas" here refers equally to the acts of exhortation, sympathetic joy, dedication, and the making of vows.
In the subsequent explanation, the first line clarifies the causal practice, namely the production of goodness and the cessation of evil.
Furthermore, the next line clarifies the resultant virtue, namely wisdom and merit.
Based on the merit produced by these methods such as repentance, no other dharma can surpass it; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed.
Furthermore, because it causes one to leave suffering and extinguish evil, it is called "complete destruction."
This means that there is no practice left unprepared and no fault left unexhausted.
All-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) likewise takes these dharmas such as repentance as its foundation; all other merits are likewise adorned by dharmas such as repentance.
This is precisely the twofold adornment of merit and wisdom.

Regarding "the eradication of all sufferings," this refers to uprooting the two types of birth and death—those of the segmented and those of transformation; this concludes the section on the transcendence of faults.
"Bestowing immeasurable bliss" refers to bestowing the two kinds of bliss—namely, *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*; this concludes the section on the perfection of virtues.
From "those with deficient faculties" onwards is the second major section, which introduces the power and function of the sutra.
Within this, there are two parts:

the first six lines conclude the preceding introduction and the main treatise of the "Chapter on Giving Up the Body," clarifying that those who propagate the sutra obtain the power and efficacy of the sutra.

The second section, "The Four World-Protecting Kings," consisting of five lines of verse below, concludes the introductory sequence from the "Chapter on the Four Kings" through the "Chapter on Vaiśravaṇa," clarifying the great power and efficacy of the scripture.

In this context, it is intended to show that those who previously propagated the sutra possessed virtue and were thus protected by celestial deities; whereas in the subsequent main exposition, it is shown that one can propagate the sutra precisely because of such divine protection. Therefore, there is a difference between the beginning and the end of the introduction and the main body of the text.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
the first three and a half lines clarify the evils to be extinguished, while the subsequent two and a half lines clarify the practice capable of extinguishing them.
Furthermore, within the first part, there are two sub-sections:
The first two lines and one phrase clarify how evil sorrow arises due to present events; the subsequent five phrases clarify how affliction arises due to future events.
Since all evil matters in the world do not exceed those that are either present or future, these two categories encompass everything.

The first phrase from the beginning down to "and so forth" (以下) applies throughout and connects to the preceding eight phrases. This is like saying: "Because the sense faculties are incomplete, there is sorrow, anxiety, and fear; because the devas have abandoned him, there is sorrow, anxiety, and fear," continuing up to "because wealth and property are depleted, there is sorrow, anxiety, and fear"—just as they apply throughout and connect [the subsequent clauses].

Regarding the second [category], malevolent stars are anomalies of the heavens; the path of insects and ghosts and spirits are anomalies of the spirit realm; and evil dreams are anomalies of dream-phenomena.
If one encounters such threefold obstacles or evil matters, by listening to the sutra with a pure mind, they will be immediately extinguished.
Regarding the three obstructions: being incomplete, diminished, afflicted by hardship, and abandonment constitute the obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
Quarreling, litigation, contention, and even grief and affliction collectively constitute the obstruction of karma and afflictions (*karmakleśāvaraṇa*).
Being subjected to harm, depletion, calamities, or evil dreams are the conditions for the arising of karmic afflictions.
If one propagates this sutra, suffering will be extinguished and happiness will arise; therefore, one is freed from the obstacle of retribution.
To extinguish evil and give rise to good is to depart from the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).
To extinguish delusion and give rise to understanding is to depart from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The second point, concerning the great power of the introductory sutra, can be understood accordingly.
Within the circulation preface, there are two parts:
the first eight lines and a half serve as a preface for the circulation of the "Life Span" chapter;
the final line of verse serves as a preface for the circulation of the sections following the "Repentance" chapter.
Question:
In this context, the Buddha himself praises the sutra, whereas the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha" (*Buddhastava-parivarta*) praises only the Buddha’s virtues. How, then, does it serve as a preface?
The commentary explains:
The reason this sutra is honored is that it expounds the virtues of the Buddha;
therefore, it praises the Buddha. This section consists of four parts:

first, one and a half lines praise the worthiness of the recipient; second, four lines of verse clarify the attainment of fruits through the propagation of the sutra; third, two lines of verse clarify the exhortation to practice; and fourth, one line of verse clarifies the person who propagates the sutra.
"Respected by the eight classes of beings and protected by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas" refers to the fruit of external protection.
The verse's phrase "immeasurable mass of merit" refers to the internal primary retribution.
"Offering with a mind of loving-kindness" means offering this sutra with a mind that bestows happiness upon sentient beings.
It is just as in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, which states, "Arousing a mind of loving-kindness for the sake of awakening"; here, it is likewise so.
There are generally three kinds of offerings:
first, the offering of material gain; second, the offering of reverence; and third, the offering of practice.
Among these, the present offering consists solely of the offering of reverence and the offering of practice.
"Human body" distinguishes it from other bodies;
"human realm" distinguishes it from other realms;
"right livelihood" distinguishes it from wrong livelihood.
By hearing this sutra and making offerings, one immediately becomes fully endowed with merit and wisdom, surpassing all others; therefore, it is said that one "attains well.
The second section, the Gate of the Causes for the Preface, can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the reason why the power and function of the sutra are not explained separately from the "Preface" (or "Introduction") below the section on the Four Kings: it is because the power and function of the sutra are fundamentally obtained through the circulation of the sutra's substance; therefore, they are not elucidated separately.
The second part is the formal exposition,
which has two sections.
First, from the "Chapter on Lifespan" through the "Chapter on Emptiness," it clarifies the eternal cause and effect, which constitutes the essence of the sutra.

Second, from the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" through the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body," it clarifies the praise of the sutra and the exhortation to study, which constitutes the power and function of the sutra.
Within the first [section], there are further two parts:
the "Chapter on Lifespan" clarifies that the three bodies are eternally abiding; this is the fruit.
From the second chapter, "The Chapter on Repentance" (*Pratikramana-parivarta*), onwards, the cultivation of the path is elucidated; this constitutes the causal practice (*hetu-caryā*).

Regarding the measure of lifespan, it takes the immeasurable as its measure; regarding the true mark of suchness (*tathatā-svalakṣaṇa*), it takes the signless as its mark; regarding the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it takes the boundless as its limit.
This chapter consists of three parts:
First, the manifestation of the four Buddhas in response to the doubts of Śraddhālakṣaṇa; they are termed "manifestation" because they descended into his chamber and displayed auspicious omens.
Second, from "At that time, Śraddhālakṣaṇa... onwards, it clarifies Śraddhālakṣaṇa’s inquiry and the exposition provided by the four Buddhas.
In the prose section following the third verse, the benefits for the assembly while seated are clarified, as well as the non-manifestation of the four Buddhas.
Within the first [section], the initial part clarifies the arising of doubt;
from the phrase "when reflecting on this meaning" onwards, it next clarifies the descent and manifestation.
Regarding the characteristic of faith (*śraddhā*): this refers to a bodhisattva prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) who has reached certainty regarding the principle; therefore, it is called "faith.

Such a person has previously made offerings to various Buddhas and deeply planted roots of merit; thus, they are able to receive the secret empowerment of the Buddhas' three mysteries and eliminate eighty kinds of doubt concerning the Buddha.
Question: At what time was this sutra spoken? [The answer is: It is suspected to be the eightieth [chapter].
Explanation:
It was spoken ninety days before his parinirvāṇa.

We know this to be so because, from the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there is no mention of an eighty-year [lifespan]; however, after preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he addressed Māra, declaring:
"Three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
At that time, sentient beings only realized it had been exactly eighty years.
From this, it can be known that the teaching was given during the ninety days; however, within those ninety days, it remained unknown on which specific day it was delivered.
"About to" (*jāng*) means "nearing.
To enter the eighty-year period on the fifteenth day of the second month, yet not having reached its full completion, is called "nearing.
The passage beginning with "He further thought again" clarifies that he contemplates the cause based on doubt regarding the result.
Abstaining from killing is the primary cause for long life, like a biological mother;
providing food is the contributory cause, like a wet nurse.
Within the second section on the descent and manifestation, it first clarifies how the four Buddhas descended into the chamber.
Below the phrase "Emitting Great Radiance," the manifestation of auspicious signs reveals the benefits received.
For what reason is the small chamber transformed into something vast, expansive, and pure?
It secretly reveals that what was short is immediately made long, just as this chamber, though defiled, is immediately purified.
The remainder may also be sought elsewhere.
From the passage beginning "At that time, Śraddhālakṣaṇa" onwards is the second major section.
Within this, it first clarifies Śraddhālakṣaṇa’s presentation of his doubts and his request for instruction.
From "At that time, the four Buddhas" onwards, it clarifies that the four Buddhas preached for him.
This section contains three parts:
first, a brief summary of the examination and exhortation;
"Then the four Tathāgatas" and below constitutes the second section, the extensive explanation of the assembly;
"Therefore, O Great Being" and the following two lines constitute the third section, the double conclusion.
In the first [section], there is first a preliminary trial;
from the words "For what reason" (*kasmāt*) onwards, the permanence [of the teaching] is briefly indicated.
In the second [section], there is first the clarification of the assembly of the multitude.
From "At that time, the four Buddhas" onwards, it is explained in detail through verses.

Although the various waters, Mount Sumeru, the great earth, and space are difficult to know, they are all phenomena possessing characteristics (*sanimitta-dharma*); thus, they can be known by the mind and can be expressed in words.

Thus, the fruit of the Buddha’s three bodies is three yet eternally one, and one yet eternally three; yet, being neither one nor three, its essence cannot be known by the intellect and its characteristics cannot be expressed in words, for it is beyond all measure, calculation, and enumeration.
Furthermore, the Dharma-body is primordially existent and devoid of arising or ceasing; the Reward-Buddha, being in correspondence with it, likewise has no arising or ceasing.
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is what is called the Dharma."
"Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal.

Furthermore, the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) Tathāgata takes the two [other] bodies as its essence and sentient beings as its condition; because this essence is inexhaustible, the Transformation Body is also inexhaustible. Therefore, it is said that the three bodies are eternally abiding.

As clarified in the seven-fascicle *Sūtra*, if the two bodies—the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the transformation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*)—are considered "continuously constant," it is because the light radiating from the front and back, marked by the thirty-two major signs and so forth, which are projected by the bodhisattva’s karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), are collectively designated as the "retribution Buddha" (*vipākabuddha*). Since these are associated with the cause of bestowing happiness upon others, they are discussed in terms of their essence as being the transformation body; therefore, it is said that they are constantly continuous from moment to moment.
If one asks: "If the retribution that accords with principle is eternally quiescent and permanent, why do the four Buddhas not appear?
It is because this reveals that the Dharma-body is non-different; although there are four manifestations in their traces, the place to which they return is no different.
The three chapters below, beginning with "Repentance" (Chān-hui), clarify the essence of the scripture.
Second is the section on the Gate of Cultivating the Path (xiū-dào mén).

Since the fruit is not attained spontaneously but must depend upon the cultivation of the path, this is explained next; it constitutes the primary teaching on the contributory cause (yuán-yīn) within the gate of causes.
If one discusses the direct cause (*hetu*), it is found within the "Chapter on the Three Bodies" (*Tri-kāya-paṭala*) of the seven-fascicle version of this sutra, though it is omitted here in brief.
Regarding this section on causes, there are two parts:
the first two chapters clarify the gate of merit (*guṇa-mukha*), which constitutes the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*).
The final chapter elucidates the gate of wisdom, which is the path of *prajñā*.
Why are these two elucidated?
Because all causal practices do not transcend merit and wisdom; thus, they are fully encompassed by these two gates.
What is the meaning of attaining the fruit of the three bodies by relying on the cultivation of two causes?

Because one cultivates merit, this is not the practice of the two vehicles; because one cultivates wisdom, this is not the practice of ordinary beings. Because it is not the practice of ordinary beings, one does not remain in saṃsāra; because it is not the practice of the two vehicles, one does not abide in nirvāṇa. This is precisely the attainment of the two bodies of the nirmāṇakāya and sāmbhogikakāya.
Because one does not remain in saṃsāra, the dharmakāya is perfected; thus, it is said that the fruit of the three bodies is attained.

Furthermore, by cultivating merit one is freed from the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), and by cultivating wisdom one is freed from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); thus, through correspondence with principle, the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is attained.
Because the obstacle of karma is abandoned, one acts without hindrance according to the needs of beings, and the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests.
Once both obstacles are abandoned, the resultant *ālayavijñāna* ceases and no longer arises, and the essence of the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*) is ultimately revealed.
Therefore, those who wish to attain the three bodies must necessarily cultivate merit and wisdom.
One may seek analogies for this by comparing it to the three points and the three natures.
Within the gate of merit, the two categories constitute two sections:
The "Chapter on Repentance" was spoken by the Buddha and recounted by Śraddhālakṣaṇa;
the "Chapter on Praise" was previously spoken by Śraddhālakṣaṇa and is now recounted by the Buddha.
For what reason are these two explained?
It is to manifest the Way of Resonance and Response.
The matters seen and heard by Śraddhālakṣaṇa in his dream were the response of the Tathāgata; therefore, Śraddhālakṣaṇa recounted them to the Buddha.
The praise of the Buddha and the making of vows recounted here are the result of the resonance of faith; therefore, the Buddha now addresses them in response to Xinxiang.
To demonstrate that seeing and hearing [the Buddha] are not in vain, he clarifies the correspondence between the response and the stimulus.
Why is it that one sees and hears within a dream?

It is to clarify that for a Bodhisattva, awakening and dreaming are no different; furthermore, it is to reveal that the Buddha-work of the Tathāgata does not depend on day or night; and finally, it is because of the power of the vows of Śraddhālakṣaṇa.

Regarding the term "Chapter on Repentance" (Chanhui pin): in foreign lands it is called *kṣamāpita*, which here means "aversion and detachment" (*yànlí*), and is also called "reform and repentance" (*gǎihuì*).
Since both the non-Chinese (Hú) and Chinese terms are preserved, it is termed "repentance" (*chànhuì*).
Within this chapter, five dharmas are fully elucidated; since repentance comes first, the title is derived from the beginning.
This chapter consists of two parts:
the initial prose section is the narration of the scribe, while the subsequent verses are the personal testimony of Śraddhālakṣaṇa.
Regarding the prose section, there are two parts:
first, the clear exposition on the signs of faith seen and heard within a dream;
second, from "After awakening from the dream" onwards, the clear exposition on how the one possessed of faith, having awakened, proceeded to the Buddha's abode to speak.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, seeing the Tathāgata as he responds;
second, seeing a person who clearly perceives the response of sentient beings.
"The very night" refers to the night when the "Chapter on the Lifespan" was finished being preached.
"Golden drum" is a metaphor for the Dharmakāya.
The word "exquisite" (shu) means "wondrous" (miao); it is wondrous because it transcends the names and marks of birth and death.
"Great" (Mahā) means that because it universally encompasses all virtues, it is called "Great.
Based on this Dharmakāya, the Nirmāṇakāya is manifested; since the Nirmāṇakāya shines everywhere, it is said to be like the light of the sun.

That which is "luminous" is the light itself, not the luminosity within the light; therefore, it corresponds to the *sambhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body) and is not a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Body).
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, within the light" clarifies that seeing the transformation Buddhas constitutes the luminosity within the light.
This clarifies that while the two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—are merely metaphors for the absence of phenomena, within the body there are phenomena for which no metaphor exists.
"Yet he preaches the Dharma" clarifies what is heard.

Regarding the phrase "resembling a Brahmin," the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa resides in the stage prior to the *bhūmis*; because he has not yet attained the true understanding of the *bhūmi* stages, he is said to "resemble" them.

The faculty of faith is like a drumstick that strikes the drum of the *dharmakāya*, causing the sounds of the *nirmāṇakāya* to emerge and preach dharmas such as repentance; therefore, it is said that "one strikes the drum with a stick" and so forth, up to the recitation of verses.
The second section, the textual characteristics of which are clear, contains two parts within its verses:
first, the initial four lines of verse describe what was seen, and the characteristics of this vision are evident; [the remainder follows].
From "Within the sound of that drum" onwards, the next section describes what was heard.
This consists of two parts:
first, a general indication in half a verse; second, a detailed exposition in one hundred and fifty-seven and a half verses.
Within this, there are four sections:
the first, consisting of seventy-six lines, clarifies the practice of avoiding faults;
the second, beginning with "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are my refuge" and extending for seventy-two and a half lines, clarifies the practice of gathering what is wholesome.
The third section, "If there are those who pay homage," consisting of six and a half verses, exhorts practice by highlighting its benefits;
the fourth section, "Not from one Buddha," consisting of two and a half lines, praises the difficulty of hearing this sutra.
The mutual generation [of these meanings] can be seen.
Regarding the first [section], there are two examples:
the initial twenty-two verses clarify the praise of the superior function of the teaching;
The second section, "Without Support or Refuge," consists of fifty-four verses that correctly clarify the essence of practice free from faults.
This section has three parts;
first, ten verses clarify the function of uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness.
The second section, consisting of eight lines of verse beginning with “If there are sentient beings dwelling in the hells,” clarifies the eradication of evil and the generation of virtuous qualities;
the third section, consisting of four lines of verse beginning with “If there are sentient beings fallen into the great hells,” provides the conclusion.
Furthermore, regarding the first section, there are two parts:
the first two verses clarify the extraction of the three kinds of suffering;
the subsequent eight verses, beginning with "That which is produced by this drum," clarify the bestowal of the three kinds of happiness.
Regarding the three kinds of suffering: first, the suffering of the three periods of time is "long-term suffering," because it is experienced for a long duration throughout the three periods.
Second, the suffering of the three miserable realms is "heavy suffering," because this suffering is coarse and burdensome.
Third, there are the sufferings of the three realms; poverty is the suffering among humans.
"And the sufferings of existence" refers to the suffering in the heavens.
Within these sufferings of the three realms, both the suffering of formation and the suffering of destruction are fully contained; this is what constitutes profound suffering.
Regarding the second [section], bestowing happiness: the first two verses clarify the bestowal of the happiness of fearlessness;
the subsequent five verses, beginning with "The Buddhas and Sages," clarify the bestowal of the happiness of bodhi;
and the final verse clarifies the bestowal of the happiness of quiescent extinction, which is the happiness of rest.
This sutra can cure all fears caused by being oppressed by general conditions, enabling one to attain the fearlessness of a Buddha.
Regarding the second term, "the bliss of bodhi," it refers to the bliss of awakened wisdom.
Among these, the first verse first clarifies that which all Buddhas have realized, in order to demonstrate that this sutra enables sentient beings to realize what the Buddhas have realized.
The subsequent four verses of the gāthā correctly clarify the bestowing of the bliss of bodhi.
Within this, the first two and a half lines clarify the bodhi of self-benefit;
the subsequent one and a half lines clarify the bodhi of benefiting others.

Regarding the phrase "the merit obtained by such sentient beings," it means that the merit obtained by these sentient beings is like that of the Buddhas; it means that the concentration and the factors conducive to enlightenment obtained by these sentient beings are like an ocean.
"Concentration" refers to the four *ārūpya-samāpattis*; "factors conducive to the Path" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and so forth.
Because it transcends practices such as the *pāramitās* and surpasses all other aids to the Path, the word "and" (*ji*) is used.
Furthermore, regarding "those who can also realize the path": this refers to the Path of Teaching transcending the Non-abiding Path; hence the word "and" (*ji*) is used.

This single line clarifies the perfection of the causes of Bodhi; since the causal practice is perfected, the fruit of Bodhi is fulfilled, and thus it says "causing them to attain the Brahma-voice and the supreme fruit."
The Brahma-voice possesses five virtues: first, it is deep like thunder;
second, it is clear and resonant, heard from afar; third, it is precise and easy to understand; fourth, all sentient beings love and revere it; and fifth, those who listen never grow weary of it.
Possessing these five virtues is called the Brahma-voice;
this is the Bodhi of the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body).
As for the "supreme fruit," this refers to the Bodhi of the Dharmakāya and Sambhogakāya (Dharma and Enjoyment Bodies).

It is clearly explained that the essence and characteristics of the transformed Buddha’s Brahma-voice are themselves self-benefit; therefore, even the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is termed the "enlightenment of self-benefit.

Once the three bodies are perfected, one turns the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma and bestows it upon sentient beings, remaining for immeasurable eons to preach the True Dharma for their ultimate benefit. Thus, it is said: "Turning the unsurpassed wheel, and so forth, benefiting sentient beings."
The third statement regarding "the bliss of quiescence" refers to the bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); its textual characteristics may be investigated accordingly.
Within the second section on "extinguishing evil and giving rise to good," there are four parts:

first, two lines clarify the arising of faith; next, two lines clarify the arising of understanding; next, two lines of verse clarify the arising of practice; and finally, two lines of verse clarify the fulfillment of aspirations.

First, regarding the generation of faith: if sentient beings suffering in the hells can still generate faith and pay homage to the Buddha upon hearing the teachings issued from this golden drum, how much more so for those among humans and devas who would not fail to receive its benefit?
Therefore, I have singled out those in the hells.

As for the statement "to give rise to understanding," it means to cause them to know the causes and effects of their own past good and evil deeds, and also to cause them to maintain right mindfulness of the Buddhas, hear the unsurpassed Dharma, and distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
To speak of "arousing practice" means to cause one to encounter the conditions for practicing the Way under the various Buddhas and to depart from evil karma.
To cause "vows to be fulfilled" means that there is nothing that is not fully endowed with faith, understanding, practice, and the fulfillment of vows.
Since the evils such as lack of faith have naturally been extinguished once these [qualities] are fully perfected, it is said that "evil is extinguished and goodness arises.

In the third summary, only the eradication of suffering is summarized; the rest are omitted. The first line cites the heavy sufferings of hell; the second line cites the long-lasting sufferings of saṃsāra; the third line summarizes the heavy sufferings of the three miserable realms and the profound sufferings within the three states of existence; the final line of the verse summarizes the extinction of suffering with the "Drum Sound" (Ghoṣadatta).
From the section "Without Support and Without Refuge" onwards is the second major division, which clarifies the practice of avoiding faults.
The essence of this practice of avoiding faults does not exceed five types.
What are these five?
These are confession, exhortation, sympathetic joy, dedication, and the making of vows.
Why does a bodhisattva practice these five dharmas? It is because they wish to overturn the mind that constitutes the root of evil.
There are also five kinds of roots from which offenses arise:

first, a mind lacking shame and remorse; second, a mind that does not delight in the Buddha-dharma; third, a mind of envy and jealousy; fourth, a mind of attachment to the three realms of existence; and fifth, a mind of indolence.
The bodhisattva’s repentance takes shame and remorse as its essence; therefore, it corresponds to the reversal of the first mind.
However, there are three types of persons regarding shame and remorse:
the first is one who feels shame before teachers and friends, committing no offenses where they are present but committing them where they are not; this is a person of inferior grade.
Second, there is shame before the Buddhas and the devas; one does not transgress when mindful, but transgresses when unmindful—this is the person of middling capacity.

Third, there is shame regarding one's own self, considering that it shares the same nature as all Buddhas; yet while the Buddhas have already realized and attained their own nature, I alone have not. Therefore, one feels shame for one's own self and refrains from committing evil deeds—this is the person of superior capacity.
The second exhortation takes the mind that delights in the Buddha and seeks the Dharma as its essence; thus, it corresponds to the reversal of the second [of the four immeasurables].
The third, sympathetic joy, takes the mind of joy among the four immeasurables as its essence; thus, it corresponds to the reversal of the third.
The fourth dedication takes the bodhicitta as its essence; therefore, it corresponds to the reversal of the fourth.
The fifth, the generation of the vow, takes the mind that aspires to benefit oneself and others as its essence; therefore, it corresponds to the reversal of the fifth.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva practices five dharmas during six periods.
Within this section, there are three parts:
first, nineteen verses which clarify repentance by way of the causes and conditions that give rise to evil.
The second section, from "I now make offerings" downward, consists of twenty-seven and a half lines, which clarifies repentance in terms of the time and occasion when evil was committed;
the third section, from "If in this land" downward, consists of seven and a half verses, which clarifies repentance based on the place where evil was done and where its retributive fruit is received.
All three obstructions do not transcend causes and conditions, time and season, and place; therefore, these three encompass everything completely.
Regarding this, the first verse clarifies the making of vows, which is the internal cause for extinguishing transgressions;
the subsequent two verses clarify the exhortation [to the Buddhas], which is the external condition for extinguishing transgressions.
The sixteen verses beginning with "What I have originally done" correctly clarify the essence of repentance.

As for why the vow is first established: the practice of a bodhisattva must necessarily take the *bodhicitta* as its basis; therefore, the various practices they cultivate differ from those of the followers of the Two Vehicles or ordinary worldlings.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The perfections of a bodhisattva have no equal as their basis.
For this reason, herein one generates the vow to act as a place of refuge for all sentient beings who lack protection and support.

Next, to explain the exhortation: although one possesses the internal causes for extinguishing transgressions, if the external superior conditions are lacking, those transgressions are difficult to remedy; therefore, it is necessary to certainly entreat the Buddhas to act as the masters of repentance and transformation, just as people in the world invite a master of confession before them.
Since the causes and conditions are thus complete, the next section clarifies the confession, the sense of shame, and the self-reproach.
Within this, the first verse provides a general confession;
from "Not recognizing the Buddhas" onwards, there is a specific confession.

Among these, the first verse clarifies that while the internal cause is not distinct from ignorance, the external conditions consist of superior reflection and the performance of wholesome deeds yet the commission of various evils.
The subsequent verse clarifies that the internal causes are pride and negligence, while the external conditions are lineage, wealth, and age.
The next verse clarifies that while the internal causes—the three types of karma—are present, external conditions do not perceive their faults.
The subsequent verse clarifies that the internal cause is ignorance, while the external condition is proximity to evil friends.
The next verse-line clarifies that the internal causes are anger and greed, while the external conditions are the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
The subsequent verse-line clarifies that the internal causes are stinginess, envy, lewdness, and flattery, while the external conditions are non-noble [beings] and poverty.
The next verse-line clarifies that the internal cause is fear, while the external condition is dependence on others.
The subsequent verse-line clarifies that the internal cause is the thirst of the three poisons, while the external conditions are all phenomena (*dharmas*).
The next verse explains that the internal causes are the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), while the external conditions are clothing, food, and female beauty.
The following verse explains the general enumeration of the three types of action (*trikarma*) and the expression of remorse and reproach.
The subsequent two verses explain that the internal causes are the three poisons and arrogance, while the external conditions are the Three Jewels and the Three Vehicles.
The next one and a half verses clarify that the internal cause is ignorance, while the external conditions are the True Dharma, parents, and teachers.
The subsequent one and a half verses provide a general summary and conclusion for the confession.
Within the second section on repentance, there are three parts.
First, the initial four and a half verses clarify that making vows constitutes the internal cause;
second, the seven verses beginning with "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones," clarify that the Buddhas constitute the external conditions.
The third section, consisting of six lines of verse beginning with "All past evils," is the actual confession.
Its structural development can be seen by analogy with what precedes it.
Regarding this first part, there are three sub-sections:
The first verse clarifies the vow to make offerings to all Buddhas above;
the second section, beginning with "I shall deliver," consisting of eight and a half verses, clarifies the vow to transform sentient beings below;
the third section, beginning with "I shall establish," consisting of five verses, clarifies the vow to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Within the second vow, there are two parts:
the first four lines express the aspiration to cause [beings] to leave suffering and attain happiness;
the subsequent four and a half verses clarify the aspiration to cause the cessation of evil and the arising of goodness.
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts:
first, one verse clarifies causing [beings] to leave suffering; next, two verses clarify causing them to attain happiness; and finally, one verse concludes with leaving suffering.
Regarding the second [section], "extinguishing evil," there are three parts:

The first verse explains the method for repentance; the next two verses teach the procedure for performing repentance; and the final one and a half verses conclude by praising the power of this sutra to extinguish obstacles.
Regarding the third vow, there are two parts within the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood:
first, the initial two lines provide a brief summary, expressing the vow to attain the fruit of Buddhahood in order to transform sentient beings;
second, the following three lines provide a detailed explanation.
"Abiding in the ten stages" refers to the essence of the ten kinds of dharma-realms.
"The ten kinds of precious jewels" refers to the practice of the ten pāramitās.
These pāramitās traversing the ten kinds of dharma-realms are called the feet.
Furthermore, the ten *pāramitās* may be considered the "feet" as causes, for they establish the fruit of Buddhahood; thus they are called "feet.
As for the "profound treasury of Dharma," it refers to the profound principle known by the Buddha, which possesses immeasurable virtues.
“Sarvākārajñatā” (All-aspect omniscience) refers to the aspiration for the fruit of wisdom.
From “hundreds of thousands of dhyānas” downward, it refers to the aspiration for the fulfillment of the fruit of merit.
Within the second major section, the Exhortation, there are three parts:
The first line provides the heading; the next four and a half lines offer the explanation; and the final one and a half lines provide the conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are two parts:
the first two and a half lines clarify the request made because [the author] possesses evil fears.
The following two lines clarify the request because the Buddha possesses great compassion and the power to cure;
the concluding request is easily understood.
Regarding the third section, the actual confession of transgressions, there are three parts:
The first two lines address the three periods of time; the next two lines address the ten unwholesome actions; and the final two lines provide a general summary and conclusion of the repentance.
In the third major section, which clarifies repentance by way of location, there are two parts:
the first two lines clarify the dedication of merit, and the subsequent five and a half lines constitute the actual repentance.

As for why dedication is explained first: its source lies in the commission of evil within the six realms of the mundane world and the subsequent experience of retribution; since this fundamentally stems from attachment to the three realms of existence, one gives rise to the mind of dedication to overturn that very root.
Regarding the second section, there are two parts:
the first three lines constitute a general confession, and the subsequent two and a half lines constitute a specific confession.
Within the first part, there are two sub-sections.
The first one and a half lines offer a general confession by citing the evil karma of the six realms of existence;
the next one and a half lines offer a general confession by citing the afflictions of birth and death.

Within the specific confessions, the phrase "light negligence" (*qingni*) refers to a mind that lacks a master, which is precisely the affliction of distraction; if this is correlated with the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), it corresponds to "worldly wisdom" (*laukika-jñāna*).

"Difficulties arising from associating with evil friends" refers to adverse conditions; if correlated with the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), these refer to non-Buddhist practitioners such as those of the Formless Heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*).

"Perils and difficulties of the three realms of existence" refers to taking birth in places where evil arises; if correlated with the eight difficulties, this refers to Uttarakuru, because there one lacks the aspiration to transcend the world.

Regarding the "difficulty of the three poisons," this refers to the arising of internal causes for evil; if these are correlated with the eight difficulties, they constitute the three miserable realms:
those with excessive delusion are born as animals, those with excessive greed fall among the hungry ghosts, and those with excessive anger enter hell.

"Difficulties that are not [actually] difficult" refers to evil retribution; if correlated with the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), this corresponds to the difficulty of having incomplete faculties.

Regarding "the difficulty of encountering a favorable time," the following clarifies the timing for committing evil; if correlated with the eight difficulties, this corresponds to being before or after a Buddha (*buddhānām pūrva-paścimam*).
Up to this point, the first section has clarified the practice of departing from faults.

Although all three obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are confessed within these three segments of repentance, if we discuss them in terms of their relative prominence and concealment: the first segment takes afflictions (*kleśa*) as its primary subject, the second takes karma (*karman*) as its primary subject, and the third takes the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*) as its primary subject. Therefore, it is also appropriate to categorize the text according to these three obstacles.
Furthermore, among the five dharmas, there are only four—repentance, exhortation, aspiration, and dedication—with the inclusion of sympathetic joy being omitted.
If one speaks according to the underlying meaning, it is subsumed within the vow to transform sentient beings below; therefore, it is not explained separately.
"‘The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are my refuge’" marks the second major section, which clarifies the practice of gathering virtuous conduct (*kuśalasaṃgraha*).
This section contains four parts;
first, twenty verses clarify the request for teaching (*adhyeṣaṇā*).
The second section, "Adorned with the Marks and Signs," consisting of forty-eight and a half verses, clarifies the making of vows.
The third section, "If in this Jambudvīpa," consisting of two lines of verse, clarifies sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).
The fourth section, beginning with "I now, by this," consists of two lines that clarify dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
There are only four dharmas; confession is omitted as it is brief, because here the focus is specifically on the inclusion of virtuous conduct (*kuśaladharmacaryā*).
In the first passage, there is no formal request for the teaching of the Right Speech; there is only language of praise.

However, when one establishes the essential meaning [of this section], the purpose of prostrating and praising is to request that [the Buddha] remain to preach the Dharma; therefore, it is called "Requesting the Teaching" (adhyeṣaṇā).
The text has two distinct parts:
the first fourteen and a half verses properly extol the Buddha's virtues;
the second part, beginning with "Like the waters of the great ocean," consists of five and a half verses that clarify this praise.

Regarding the phrase "cannot be attained" below, within the first section of praise, it does not exceed the two bodies of *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). If the praise concerns physical form (*rūpa*), it is a praise of the *nirmāṇakāya*; if the praise concerns great wisdom, great compassion, and so forth, it is a praise of the *saṃbhogakāya*. The characteristics of these textual passages may be sought accordingly.
The second section, on the adornment of the marks and signs, consists of five parts.
The first verse serves as a general aspiration for both oneself and others; the phrase "may all beings attain" indicates that the self and sentient beings constitute a single assembly.
The second section, consisting of nine verses beginning with "By my virtuous karma," is specifically for making vows for oneself.
The third section, consisting of thirty-four and a half verses beginning with "In all worlds," is specifically for making vows for others.
The text itself consists of two parts:
the first twelve and a half verses clarify the vow to uproot suffering;
the subsequent twenty-two verses, beginning with "Sentient beings gaze at one another," clarify the vow to bestow happiness.
The fourth section, from "If I, in the present... down to the next two lines of verse, concludes with the vow made for oneself.
The fifth section, from "If all sentient beings... down to the next two lines of verse, concludes with the vow made for others.
The textual form of the "rejoicing and dedication" (*anumodanā-pariṇāmanā*) is clear and may be understood accordingly.
This concludes the section on the "comprehension of virtuous conduct. From this point onward, for six and a half verses, is the third major section: "Citing Benefits to Encourage Practice."
Within this, there are two parts:
the first two stanzas clarify the cultivation of causes and the avoidance of faults, while the subsequent four and a half verses clarify the attainment of results through the cultivation of causes.
The fourth major section praises the difficulty of hearing this sutra; its textual structure is clear.
*Chapter on Praise*: Within the section clarifying the gates of merit, this is the third instance where the past discourse of Śraddhālakṣaṇa is now recounted by the Buddha.
There are two purposes for its inclusion:
first, to verify the dreams and visions experienced during the *Chapter on Repentance*, which arose through the power of Śraddhālakṣaṇa’s past praise and aspiration.
The second [section] praises the fact that what was seen and heard in the dream is not a false manifestation;
these two [sections] demonstrate the resonance and correspondence between the response and the invocation.
The general purport of this chapter fully expounds five dharmas, but because the praise comes first, the chapter is named after its initial section.
This section has three parts:

first, the prose passage introduces the person capable of praising; second, sixty and a half verses correctly describe the events such as the praise of the Buddha by Śraddhālakṣaṇa in the past; third, the final two lines clarify the connection between the ancient and the present.

Why is it that the matters concerning the aspect of faith are specifically addressed to the Earth Deity? It is because this Earth Deity has a karmic connection [with the Buddha], and therefore he addresses her alone.
Within the verses there are three parts;
the first thirteen verses clarify the act of praise, which is itself an exhortation.
The second section, beginning with "I now with reverence," consists of two lines of verse that clarify dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
The third section, beginning with "Such a king of men," consists of twenty-five and a half lines of verse that clarify the making of vows (*praṇidhāna*).
If these are categorized according to their meaning, rejoicing is included within the sections on dedication and the making of vows, while repentance is subsumed within the other vow sections.
Within the first section on praise, there are three parts:

first, one verse that praises in general; second, twenty-six and a half verses beginning with "The Buddhas are pure," which provide detailed and specific praise; and third, five and a half verses beginning with "Even if one had a hundred tongues," which clarify that the praise is inexhaustible.
Regarding the second section, the extensive praise, there are two parts:
first, twenty-three and a half verses that clarify the actual praise; second, three verses that clarify the offering of the three karmas.

In the "Extensive Praise of the Correct," his physical attributes—complexion, voice, hair, teeth, eyes, tongue, ūrṇā-kośa, eyebrows, fine features, high nose, attainment of flavor, and body hair—are each praised in succession with one verse per attribute.

From the passage "At the very moment of birth" onwards, each aspect is praised individually: the radiance emitted at birth to benefit sentient beings, the brilliance of his physical form and facial features, his majestic deportment, the halo encircling his arms, the pure and wondrous qualities of the Buddha-body, the towering splendor of the Buddha-light, and the universal illumination of the Buddha-sun.
"From what has been cultivated from the beginning" and below separately cite his own lineage and praise the color of his arms, hands, and feet.
The three types of karmic offerings cannot fully exhaust the praise; as for the dedication of merit, the textual characteristics are clear enough to understand.
From the passage beginning "Such a king of men" below, the third section clarifies the making of vows.
Within this, the first line concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one; the following twenty-four and a half lines properly clarify the making of the vows.
Within this, there are ten vows, which constitute ten sections:
the first consists of two verses, expressing the vow to dream of a golden drum and hear the sound of repentance.
The second section, beginning with "Now that which is praised," consists of one verse, expressing the aspiration to obtain the pure countenance of the Tathāgata.
The third section, beginning with "The merits of all Buddhas," consists of two verses, expressing the aspiration to see the Tathāgata in dreams and to speak of him as he truly is during the day.
From "I shall fulfill" onwards is the fourth section, consisting of two verses, which expresses the aspiration to practice the six perfections by placing others before oneself.
Although there is a separate textual passage stating "may I attain Buddhahood," the phrase "may I realize the Way" used here carries the same intent: to prioritize others over oneself.

Below the section "Offering Golden Drums," the fifth part consists of two and a half verses, expressing the aspiration to encounter Śākyamuni and receive his prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Below the section "If there are sentient beings," the sixth part consists of three verses, expressing the aspiration to serve as a place of refuge for all sentient beings.
From "In my future [lives]" onwards is the seventh section, consisting of two and a half verses, in which one vows that the ocean of afflictions and karma shall be exhausted without remainder.
Within this, the first verse is a vow to practice the path, while the subsequent one and a half verses constitute the formal aspiration.
From "My Ocean of Merit" downward, the eighth section consists of five and a half verses, expressing the vow to attain the complete endowment of all the Tathāgata’s virtues.
From "When I Shall Deliver Sentient Beings" downward, the ninth section consists of one verse, expressing the vow to uproot the suffering of sentient beings and bestow happiness upon them.
From "In many kalpas of future lives" onwards is the tenth section, which consists of three verses wishing to attain a pure land like that of the Buddhas.
The first verse is a vow to practice the path, while the latter two verses constitute the actual aspiration.
The beginning of all vows should consist of vowing to practice the Way; it is simply that the text is abbreviated and lacks this explicit statement.
From "You, O faithful one, should know" onwards is the third section: two verses that synthesize and reconcile the ancient and the modern.
Regarding the phrase "Silver Appearance" (*rūpyalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, this refers to the Silver Appearance and Silver Light mentioned below in the "Chapter on Prophecy" (*vyākaraṇaparivarta*).

In the "Chapter on Emptiness" (*śūnyatāparivarta*), which clarifies that Prajñāpāramitā guides the preceding merits, there are forty-five verses divided into three parts: first, four and a half verses introduce the intent of the brief exposition; [the second part consists of twenty-one verses on the emptiness of all phenomena;
and the third part consists of nineteen verses on the emptiness of the non-existence of all phenomena].
The second section, consisting of twenty-eight verses beginning with "This body is false," correctly explains the principle of emptiness;
the third section, consisting of twelve and a half verses beginning with "I sever all [attachments]," clarifies the benefits of contemplating emptiness in order to encourage its cultivation.
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts:

first, one line indicates that what is now being briefly explained; second, one and a half lines explain the intent of this brief explanation; third, two lines clarify that this brief explanation is intended to accord with the capacities of sentient beings who are to be benefited.

Regarding the phrase "other immeasurable sūtras," this refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras which extensively clarify that all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent, internal or external—are entirely empty and quiescent; therefore, they are said to provide an extensive exposition.
In this present sutra, only the existence of dharmas and their emptiness of internal dharmas is explained; therefore, it is called a brief exposition.
Furthermore, the intent behind being extensive or brief cannot be fixed.
If one speaks in terms of principle, the extensive version is for those of sharp faculties, while the brief version is for those of dull faculties.
If we discuss this in terms of the teachings, the extensive [version] is for those of dull faculties, while the concise [version] is for those of sharp faculties.

Furthermore, regardless of whether it concerns the teachings or the principle, the extensive [version] is for those of sharp faculties and the concise [version] is for those of dull faculties; this is because those of dull faculties lack the power of dhāraṇī and possess little wisdom.
Now, the intent here is summarized in the third line alone.
Within this third section, the first line identifies the capacity of the audience (*jñeya*), and the subsequent line expounds the teaching.

Regarding the phrase "extraordinary and wondrous skillful means" (*vicitra-upāya*): it clarifies that this current abbreviated exposition differs from the former extensive exposition; because its efficacy accords with the capacities of sentient beings, it is called "extraordinary and wondrous."
"Various causes and conditions" refers to the various matters explained in the subsequent text.
Because a detailed exposition would be of no benefit while a concise one would be beneficial, it is said that he "arouses great compassion."

"As for the phrase 'as I understand it,' this means that although this sublime scripture is spoken according to direct realization, I am merely aware of the beings' inclination toward brevity and am unable to explain it extensively."
From "This body is false and deceptive" onwards is the second section, which correctly elucidates the principle of emptiness.
This contains two parts:
first, twenty-one verses that clarify the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); [the remainder clarifies the emptiness of phenomena].
The second section, consisting of seven verses beginning from "Thus these great [elements]," clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This section has two parts:
first, nineteen and a half lines separately clarify the five gates of impermanence;...
Second, from the passage "Good daughter, you should contemplate" onwards, it clarifies the conclusion of the contemplation on emptiness.

Regarding the five gates of impermanence: it clarifies that the bodies of sentient beings are without self, impermanent, empty, suffering, and impure; this is the contemplation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The body is likewise thus; where is there a person?
Its fundamental nature is empty and quiescent—this is the contemplation of the True Dharma.
The five gates of impermanence (*anitya*) are divided into five sections:
The first four and a half lines clarify the gate of non-self:
"The body is like an empty village where the thieves of the fetters reside; there is no true master," which immediately dispels and distances the notion of self.

All the faculties each abide in their own nature and cannot cognize one another; each takes its own object as its condition and cannot take the objects of others as conditions; they possess no autonomy—this is precisely the negation of the self.
The second section, consisting of five verses beginning with "The mind is like an illusion," clarifies the gate of impermanence.

Mental consciousness is like an illusion, arising and ceasing of its own accord; it gallops through discursive thought and is harmed by the six sense objects. Furthermore, it constantly relies upon the six faculties and their respective objects, remaining in each of its watchful stations. Wherever it is, it perishes and cannot reach another place, just as a bird that falls into a fine net dies immediately.
Third, from the line "the body is empty and false" onwards, two and a half lines clarify emptiness.

To say the body is false means that although one possesses clothing and food, there is nothing therein to be nurtured; furthermore, there is no self to engage in disputes with others, nor is there any intrinsic nature that serves as the master of the body. Rather, it arises through the false appearances of causes and conditions, like a wooden puppet operated by mechanisms.
The fourth section, consisting of the four lines of verse beginning with "earth, water, fire, and wind," elucidates the gate of suffering (*duḥkha*).

The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are in mutual conflict: wind and fire ascend, while earth and water descend. Furthermore, because wind and fire are of a yang nature and tend toward the east and south, whereas earth and water are of a yin nature and tend toward the west and north, it is said that the directions also consist of two pairs.
The fifth section, consisting of three and a half verses beginning from "The two natures of mind and consciousness," elucidates the gate of impurity (*aśubha*).

The first one and a half verses clarify the impurity of the seeds (*bīja-aviśuddhi*): "mind" here refers to the *ālayavijñāna*, while the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are restless; they give rise to the impure seeds of karmic afflictions (*kleśa*) and receive bodies within the six realms of existence. Therefore, it is called the impurity of the seeds.
The subsequent verse clarifies the impurity of external appearances (*bāhya-lakṣaṇa-aviśuddhi*).
