The following half-verse clarifies ultimate impurity.
The section beginning with "Good daughter, you should contemplate" constitutes the second part, which elucidates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); the textual structure is easily understood.

The section beginning with “In this way, these great [elements]” constitutes the second major division, which clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Within this, the first two verses clarify the emptiness of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), while the subsequent five verses clarify the emptiness of both material and mental phenomena (*rūpa-citta-dharma*).
"Nature has no combination" means that the four great elements are fundamentally non-arising.

"Because there is nothing [substantial], it is conventionally named ignorance" means that when one investigates the essence of ignorance, it is precisely the true suchness (tathatā) and pure mind; where else could there be a separate essence or characteristic of ignorance?
Therefore, provisional names are termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*), just as waves are nothing other than water.
From the passage beginning with "I shall sever all [afflictions]" onwards is the third major section, which cites benefits to encourage practice.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, eight and a half verses, which exhort practice by citing the benefits of the fruit;
second, the four verses beginning with "Throughout immeasurable kalpas," which exhort practice by citing the benefits of the cause.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
the first two verses clarify the fruit of self-benefit, and the subsequent six and a half verses clarify the fruit of benefiting others.

As for the phrase "I have severed all," it means that the fruit of my own Buddhahood, Śākyamuni, was attained by severing the fetters of views and other afflictions through the contemplation of the principle of emptiness. You, too, should desire to sever these afflictions and should cultivate the contemplation of emptiness; therefore, this is called an exhortation to practice.
"The phrase 'This is the virtue of abandonment' and what follows expresses the intent of the exhortation; other instances may be sought by analogy.
The line beginning with 'The five aggregates as a dwelling' explains the fruit of the virtue of wisdom."
The second section, clarifying the fruit of benefiting others, contains two parts:
first, two and a half verses clarify the fruit of turning the wheel of Dharma; second, four verses clarify the fruit of gathering and transforming sentient beings.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, one and a half lines clarify the transformation according to principle; second, one line of verse clarifies the transformation according to teaching.
The phrase "opening the gate of ambrosia" and so forth refers to those who transform others.
Briefly stated, this is called "opening," while detailed and exhaustive analysis is called "showing.
Ambrosia is a metaphor for the fruit of *nirvāṇa*; just as people in the world who consume celestial ambrosia obtain the fruit of birth and death, so it is with *nirvāṇa*.
The four lines beginning with "Entering the City of Ambrosia" are spoken in reference to those who are to be converted.
The first line clarifies the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Entering the city refers to the wisdom of hearing when it has not yet attained realization; dwelling in the chamber refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) as it approaches realization; and tasting the flavor refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) upon attaining realization.

Regarding the "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" (*kaishijōnyū*) taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: the "opening and showing" in that sūtra is identical to the "opening and showing" in this sūtra; what that sūtra calls "entering" is termed "the locus of entry" (*nyūsho*) in this sūtra; and what that sūtra calls "awakening" is termed "tasting the flavor" (*shokumi*) in this sūtra.

Regarding "blowing the dharma-conch": just as people in the world must blow a conch when they wish to change the era name, so too does the Tathāgata; wishing to change the names and phrases of the Hīnayāna, he necessarily expounds the teachings of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding "beating the Dharma drum": just as the sound of a worldly drum is heard both near and far, enabling one to break the enemy with a unified mind, so too is the teaching of the Mahāyāna; it causes all who hear it to enter the supreme realm and destroy the enemy of afflictions. Therefore, it is called "beating the drum."

Regarding the phrase "kindling the lamp of the Dharma": just as a worldly lamp illuminates all things so that everyone may see them, so too does the Buddha; by preaching the Mahāyāna and clarifying all dharmas, he enables [beings] to attain omniscience (sarvajñatā), and is therefore called "Kindler of the Lamp" (Dīpaṃkara).
"Raining down the Dharma-rain" means that just as rain in the world causes the five grains to grow, so too does the Buddha's teaching cause roots of goodness to increase;
this is the interpretation according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*.
The section beginning with "I cause them to be subdued" clarifies the second point: the fruit of virtue in benefiting others.
Within this, the first verse clarifies the virtue of subduing the heterodox, which is the vanquishing of the celestial Māras;
the subsequent three verses clarify the virtue of uprooting suffering, which is the transformation of the six realms of existence.
From "Throughout immeasurable kalpas" onwards is the second major section, which exhorts practice by citing the benefits of the causes.
Within this, there are two parts:

first, two verses clarify the ability to perform what is difficult to perform; therein, half a verse clarifies cultivation over a long duration, the next half-verse clarifies reverent cultivation, the next half-verse clarifies uninterrupted cultivation, and the final half-verse clarifies other forms of cultivation—these being the four types of cultivation mentioned in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

The second section contains two verses clarifying the ability to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish. The first three lines clarify internal giving; the next line clarifies both internal and external giving; and the final verse clarifies external giving.

*The Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings*: Above, the first part, which elucidates the essence of the sutra, is concluded. From this chapter downward, there are twelve chapters; these constitute the second main section, which elucidates the power and function of the sutra.
Since the power of the eternally abiding cause and effect has been fully revealed, how could it not be great? Therefore, the next section clarifies this.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, five chapters clarify the greatness of the sutra’s power and exhort beings to propagate and transmit it.
Next, the seven chapters following the "Chapter on the Righteous Discourse" clarify how those capable of propagating [the teaching] obtain the power of this sutra to fulfill the preceding intent.
Within these, the first five chapters consist of two parts:

the first chapter clarifies the vow of the Four Heavenly Kings to propagate this sutra; the subsequent four chapters clarify the benefits bestowed upon those who propagate and transmit it by the eight classes of beings.

Furthermore, as for the Four Heavenly Kings, they dwell on the four terraces of Mount Sumeru known as Mount Nandikara, which is forty-two thousand yojanas above the earth, and its length and breadth are likewise the same.
Above are the Four Kings:

the Heavenly King of the East is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which is translated here as "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó). He leads the hosts of devas, along with two classes of spirits: the gandharvas and the piśācas.
The Heavenly King of the South is named Virūḍhaka, which in this language means "Increase"; he presides over the hosts of devas, as well as the two classes of spirits, the kumbhāṇḍas and the pīśācas.

The Heavenly King of the Western Quarter is named Virūpākṣa, which in this language means "Diverse Speech"; he leads the hosts of devas as well as the two classes of spirits, the nāgas and the pūtanas.
The Heavenly King of the North is named Vaiśravaṇa, which in this [language] means "Much-Hearing" (Duowen). He leads the hosts of devas as well as the two classes of spirits, yakṣas and rākṣasas;
therefore, it is called the Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings.
This chapter contains three sections.
First, it clarifies that the Four Heavenly Kings vow to propagate [the teaching].
Because the Tathāgata has affirmed the great power of the sūtra’s efficacy, the Four Heavenly Kings vow to propagate it.
Because the aspiration is vast and accordant with principle, the Buddha recounted it.

Following the second recitation of the verses, the text clarifies that the Four Kings praised the Buddha and the Tathāgata praised the Sūtra. Because he was able to preach the Sūtra, the Four Kings praised the Buddha; because the Sūtra can bring people to fulfillment, the Buddha praised the Sūtra.

The prose following the third verse clarifies that the Four Kings joyfully made offerings and formed vows; this is because, through the power of hearing the sutra, they gave rise to a great heart of joy and made offerings to the Buddha while forming their vows.
Regarding the first section, there are three parts:
first, identifying the person capable of propagating [the teaching];
second, from the words "addressed the Buddha" onwards, praising the Dharma that is to be propagated; and third... [text continues].

The third section, beginning with "This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*," clarifies that the Dharma is propagated by people. Within this third section, there are two parts: first, praising the profound virtue of the sutra; second, [the praise of the merit of the listeners]. Regarding the first part, there are three sections. First, praising the profound virtue of the sutra. This consists of three points: first, praising the profound virtue of the sutra through its title; second, praising the profound virtue of the sutra through its name; and third, praising the profound virtue of the sutra through its merits. Regarding the first point, praising the profound virtue of the sutra through its title: the title of this sutra is called *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra-rāja*. Why is it called *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*? Because it is the supreme among all dharmas, and because it illuminates all dharmas. Why is it called *Sūtra-rāja*? Because it is the king of all sutras. Why is it called *Rāja*? Because it is the sovereign over all dharmas. Why is it called *Sūtra*? Because it is the path for all sentient beings. Why is it called *Dharma*? Because it is the medicine for all sentient beings. Why is it called *Paryāya*? Because it is the gate to all dharmas. Why is it called *Nirdeśa*? Because it explains all dharmas. Why is it called *Mahāyāna*? Because it is the vehicle for all bodhisattvas. Why is it called *Vaipulya*? Because it is the vastness of all dharmas. Why is it called *Buddha-bhāṣita*? Because it is spoken by all Buddhas. Why is it called *Anuttara*? Because it is unsurpassed by any other dharma. Why is it called *Samyak-saṃbuddha-bhāṣita*? Because it is correctly and perfectly realized by all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-loka-anugrahaka*? Because it benefits all worlds. Why is it called *Sarva-duḥkha-praśamana*? Because it pacifies all sufferings. Why is it called *Sarva-puṇya-samuccaya*? Because it gathers all merits. Why is it called *Sarva-vidyā-mantra-siddhi-kara*? Because it accomplishes all vidyā-mantras. Why is it called *Sarva-vighna-vināśana*? Because it destroys all obstacles. Why is it called *Sarva-kāma-saṃpādaka*? Because it fulfills all desires. Why is it called *Sarva-dharmānupraveśa*? Because it enters into all dharmas. Why is it called *Sarva-jñatā-prāpaka*? Because it leads to the attainment of omniscience. Why is it called *Sarva-sattva-paritrāṇa*? Because it protects all sentient beings. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-anumodita*? Because it is rejoiced in by all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-deva-nāga-yakṣa-gandharva-asura-garuḍa-kinnara-mahoraga-abhyarcita*? Because it is worshipped by all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-adhiṣṭhita*? Because it is sustained by the empowerment of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-dharma-saṃgraha*? Because it encompasses all Buddha-dharmas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-viṣaya*? Because it is the domain of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-gocara*? Because it is the range of activity of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-avabhāsa*? Because it is the illumination of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-udaya*? Because it is the arising of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-niṣṭhā*? Because it is the ultimate goal of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-pariniṣpanna*? Because it is perfected by all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-parigṛhīta*? Because it is embraced by all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-anujñāta*? Because it is authorized by all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-samatā*? Because it is the equality of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-aviśeṣa*? Because it is without distinction among all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-advaya*? Because it is non-dual with all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-ekarasa*? Because it has the same flavor as all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-mārga*? Because it is the single path of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-yāna*? Because it is the single vehicle of all Buddhas.

Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-kāya*? Because it is the single body of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-citta*? Because it is the single mind of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-jñāna*? Because it is the single wisdom of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-vāk*? Because it is the single speech of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-karma*? Because it is the single activity of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-dharmatā*? Because it is the single nature of reality of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-tathatā*? Because it is the single suchness of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-bhūtatā*? Because it is the single reality of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-dharmadhātu*? Because it is the single dharma-realm of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-ākāśa*? Because it is the single space of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-śūnyatā*? Because it is the single emptiness of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-prakṛti*? Because it is the single intrinsic nature of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-lakṣaṇa*? Because it is the single characteristic of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-vyañjana*? Because it is the single phoneme of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-artha*? Because it is the single meaning of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-dharma*? Because it is the single dharma of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-svabhāva*? Because it is the single self-nature of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-śānti*? Because it is the single peace of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-nirvāṇa*? Because it is the single nirvana of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-mokṣa*? Because it is the single liberation of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-vimukti*? Because it is the single deliverance of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-viśuddhi*? Because it is the single purity of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-viśuddhatā*? Because it is the single state of purity of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-viśuddhi-gati*? Because it is the single path of purity of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha-eka-viśuddhi-viṣaya*? Because it is the single sphere of purity of all Buddhas. Why is it called *Sarva-buddha
The second section, beginning with "This sutra can illuminate," praises the manifold capabilities of the sutra.
It clarifies that because of its manifold capabilities, its merit is weighty; and because its merit is weighty, it possesses manifold capabilities.
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts:
first, the fact that all Buddhas cherish and value it, clarifying that this sutra reveals the cause for the perfection of inherent nature;
second, the fact that all devas pay homage, clarifying that the sutra generates the path for the cultivation of perfected virtue.
The third section, "The Four Kings Praise the Buddha," clarifies that the cultivation of merit results in the realization of the sutra.

Regarding the first part, it begins by extolling the Dharma as being like the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light): the causal nature of the *dharmakāya* is like gold, the causal nature of *prajñā* is like light, and the causal nature of *vimukti* is like clarity; thus, the Buddha-nature of the three bodies is also attained through these analogies.
Next, the passage beginning with "All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones" clarifies the person; this person is the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) of all Buddhas.
To take the Dharma as one's teacher is expressed by the term "protective mindfulness.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma."
In the second [section], there is likewise first a praise of the Dharma.
Because the Dharma is able to give rise to the path of bodhisattva practice, it is said: "Adorning the profound and wondrous merits of the bodhisattvas."
Next, the person is explained.
Because a person can practice the Path according to the teaching, they are revered by all the devas.
From the words "can cause" onwards is the third section, which likewise first praises the Dharma.
The Dharma accomplishes the four virtues, causing all devas to aspire to it with joy; therefore, it is called "rejoicing.
Next, the human realm is explained:
because the human mind rejoices, they praise it with their mouths; therefore, it is said that it is "also praised by others."
Regarding the second section, "The Sūtra on the Many Capabilities of Sighing," there are three parts:
first, the generation of wisdom, because it illuminates the royal palaces to cause the arising of wisdom;
next, the bestowing of happiness; and finally, the clarification of the cessation of suffering.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a detailed explanation;
from "Summarizing the Essentials" onwards, a general conclusion.
There are seven kinds of suffering within the separate realms: namely, the three miserable paths, fear, enemies and bandits, famine, illness, malevolent stars, and anxiety and distress.
From the passage "The World-Honored One is the Golden Light" onwards is the third major section, in which the Dharma is propagated by humans.
It has two parts:
first, clarifying how the Four Heavenly Kings hear the sutra and obtain benefits;...
The second section, beginning with "We, the Four Kings, are able to preach the True Dharma," expresses the vow to propagate [the teaching].
This vow to propagate it arises because of the benefits gained therefrom.
The phrase "the mind is courageous and sharp" clarifies wisdom.
Within the second section, there are five parts, which are broadly divided into two categories:
the first part clarifies how the Four Heavenly Kings voluntarily offer protection, which the Buddha then confirms and completes.
There are four sections on exhorting others to propagate [the teaching], with the Tathāgata providing his endorsement.
Regarding the first, there are two parts:
first, the King’s vow to protect; second, the Tathāgata’s endorsement.
Regarding the first [section], there are again two parts:
first, the Four Kings themselves clarify their own virtue of extensive protection; second, from "If in this land... onwards, they formally make their vows.
"Capable of expounding" refers to being able to expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
"Cultivation" refers to the six perfections.
These two phrases clarify the supramundane virtues.
The section beginning with "Acting as the Dharma King of the World" clarifies his worldly virtues.
Governing the world according to the Dharma and warding off various evil spirits and the like constitute his worldly virtues.
Within the second section on the formal making of vows, there are two parts:
first, the vow to protect the nation;
second, from the words "Just as the various kings" onwards, the vow to protect sentient beings.
Regarding the description of the second Buddha, there are two parts:
first, the praise;
second, the formal description beginning with "proclaiming the True Dharma."

Regarding the initial statement that the Four Kings made offerings to the Buddhas of the past: these Four Kings have attained the rank of the First Bhūmi and have practiced their conduct for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
"Planting various roots of goodness" refers to the mind that transcends the world.

As stated in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*: "In the first bhūmi one becomes a Caturmahārājika king; in the second bhūmi, a Trāyastriṃśa king; in the third bhūmi, a Yāma king; in the fourth bhūmi, a Tuṣita king; in the fifth bhūmi, a Nirmāṇarati king; and in the sixth bhūmi, a Paranirmitavaśavartin king."
In the seventh stage is the first dhyāna; in the eighth stage, the second dhyāna; in the ninth stage, the third dhyāna; and in the tenth stage, the fourth dhyāna.
After ten such cycles, one becomes a Golden Wheel-turning King, ruling over the four continents.
"In the stage of the Ten Practices, one is a silver-wheel-turning monarch (rājā cakravartin) who rules over three worlds;
in the stage of the Ten Understandings, one is a copper-wheel-turning monarch who rules over two worlds;
in the stage of the Ten Faiths, one is an iron-wheel-turning monarch who rules over one world."
Regarding the second section, the actual exposition, there are two parts:
first, the exposition establishing the possession of merit;
from the words "For this reason" onwards, the exposition establishes the protection of vows, rather than the benefits gained from hearing the Dharma.
Regarding the second section on the description of vows and protection, first the second type of person who provides protection is described.
From the passage beginning with "If you all can... onwards, the first type of protection for the state is again described; the textual structure is easily understood.
Regarding the second set of four exhortations to propagate [the teaching] to others, there are three parts:

first, one section that directly exhorts others to propagate the sutra; next, two sections that demonstrate the methods for propagating the sutra; and finally, one section that clarifies gain and loss to conclude the exhortation.
The Bodhisattva not only practices this himself, but also desires to transform others; therefore, he first exhorts others to propagate the sutra.
Since propagating the sutra necessarily requires a method, he next demonstrates that method.
Once the method is known, failure to practice leads to loss, while practicing leads to gain; therefore, the next section clarifies gain and loss.
Within the first part, the initial four kings offer exhortations, followed by the Tathāgata’s exposition.
The first part, "The Initial Exhortations of the Four Kings," contains two sections:
first, the exhortation for kings to propagate the sutra;
second, from "By these causes and conditions" onwards, the clarification of the Four Kings' protection.
Within this, there are two parts.
The first concerns the four kings hearing the Dharma and attaining benefit; the matter of their attaining benefit is as described above.
The second, from the passage beginning "Therefore we... onwards, clarifies that the human king is protected.
Within this, there are three parts:

first, the protection of the Dharma; second, from "one should also" onwards, the protection of persons; and third, from "other regions" onwards, the protection of the nation. Within the protection of the nation, there are three further sections.
The first part is the introduction; next, from "If there is a king of men" onwards is the explanation; and from "giving rise to various fears and anxieties" onwards is the conclusion. Question:
Since the Sūtra and the original intent of the Four Heavenly Kings are fundamentally for the benefit of others, why does it cause suffering to arise in that country?
The commentary states:
The sutra and the Four Heavenly Kings have no intention of collectively encompassing all lands; rather, when the sutra is propagated in this land, it is in this land that there is virtue.
If those kings harbor evil intentions and oppose this virtue, they merely bring their own misfortune upon themselves, just as a person with an evil heart opposes the Buddha or their parents.
The textual characteristics are easily understood.
Within the second section, the account of the Buddhas, there are two parts:
first, for approximately twenty lines, it initially recounts the protection provided by the second set of the Four Kings;
From the passage beginning with "If in future ages" onwards, the second section recounts how the first king propagated the sutra.
This section consists of three parts;
the first describes the accomplishment of the first protection of the Dharma.
Second, from "and all kings of men" onwards, the second protection of persons is established;
third, from "furthermore, it can protect" onwards, the third protection of the land is established.
There are three parts to the protection of the land:
first, a brief exposition; second, a detailed exposition beginning from "The Four Kings should know"; and third, a conclusion beginning from "By these causes and conditions."
The textual characteristics are clear and can be understood.
Regarding the second section, which provides a formal exposition:
first, the Universal Monarch who propagates the sutra;
Second, from "This king shall immediately... onwards, the Heavenly King attains benefit;
third, from "These various human kings... onwards, there is an exhortation for human kings to propagate the sutra, which fulfills the first [section];
fourth, from "By these causes and conditions... onwards, there is an exhortation for the Heavenly King to provide protection, which fulfills the second [section].
The textual characteristics are easily understood.
Regarding the second major section, there are two parts, which are as follows:
the first part demonstrates the method for propagating the sutra; the second part demonstrates the method for applying the mind.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, the exhortation by the Four Kings; second, the narration by the Tathāgata.
Regarding the first [of these], there are again two parts:
First, the fruit and retribution are presented; second, from the passage "Such a king of men" onwards, the cultivation of causes is clarified.
Within this, there are two parts:

first, the clarification of the gravity of the Dharma; second, from the passage "Toward the teacher of the Dharma" onwards, the clarification of reverence for the person. The textual structure is easily understood.
In the second description of the Buddha, only the first causal practice is described, not the attainment of the fruit.

Within the description of the causes, the second—respecting persons—is described first; following this, from the phrase "toward the Dharma-preacher," the reverence for the Dharma is described, the textual structure of which is easily understood.
Within the second section, there are two parts:
first, the exhortation by the Four Kings; second, the narration by the Tathāgata.
Within the first part, there are two sub-sections:

First, it shows the mental application of listening to the Dharma; second, from the passage "World-Honored One, these are all kings of men" onwards, it shows the mental application of making offerings.
Question: Since the Four Heavenly Kings are of the first bhūmi or above, why does the text describe their merit in relation to human kings?
The commentary states:
This is merely a manifested trace (nirmāṇakāya) intended to cause sentient beings to look up with devotion and generate supreme merit;
the textual structure is clear enough to follow.
Regarding the description of the second Buddha, it describes only the mental application of making offerings and does not describe the mental application of listening to the Dharma.
Within this description, there are two parts:
first, the description of the human-king’s offering by Śākyamuni in this land;

The second section, from "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, hearing this wondrous sound" onwards, clarifies how the Buddhas of other directions praise the fourfold assembly for propagating the sutra.
This section has two parts:
first, it clarifies that the light does not merely illuminate the celestial palaces, but reaches as far as the great trichiliocosm.

The second section, from "These kings of men, holding incense burners in their hands" onwards, clarifies that they do not merely reach the great trichiliocosm, but also pervade the Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions.
Regarding the second section, the Praise from Other Directions, there are two parts:
first, clarifying how hearing and seeing give rise to miraculous transformations; second, the praise beginning from "With one voice in unison" (*ekavāg ekasvara*).
Within this, there are two parts:
first, praising the fourfold assembly for propagating the sutra; second, from "At that time, in the ten directions" onwards, praising the fourfold assembly for attaining the fruits.
Within this [second part], there are two sections:
The first praise concerns what is to be attained; the second, from the passage "You have already been able to sit," praises what has already been attained.
Because the fruit is spoken of within the context of the cause, it is termed "already attained."
"The twelve kinds of practice" refers to the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
"The unsurpassed Dharma drum," and so forth, refers to the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
This concludes the third major section, which clarifies gain and loss through a single instance.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the exhortation and encouragement by the Four Kings; second, the narration by the Tathāgata.
Regarding the first, there are two sub-sections:

First, the section beginning with "The Superior Human King" records the propagation of the sutra; second, from "I, out of reverent mindfulness" onwards, it records the celestial beings listening and receiving [the teaching].

Regarding the phrase "practicing together in one path": this means that the Human King who propagates the sutra practices the Mahāyāna together with the Four Heavenly Kings; therefore, they are called "one path."
There is no contradiction; this is called "concordant practice.
Furthermore, because this king of men propagates the sutra and benefits the four heavens, he is called a "donor" (*dānapati*).
From the passage beginning with "If there is a king of men," the second section correctly concludes the exhortation.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, it clarifies that those who do not propagate the sutra incur the loss of national ruin;
second, from the passage "If there is a king who wishes to protect himself," it clarifies that those who propagate the sutra obtain the gain of a prosperous land.
The third section, from "For this reason" onwards, formally concludes the exhortation to practice.
Within this, there are four parts;
the first clarifies the failure to propagate the sutra.
1. From "We, the Four Kings... onwards, it clarifies the loss of benefit for the Four Kings;
2. From "We, the Four Kings... onwards, it clarifies how the various devas abandon the kingdom;
3. From "In that country there shall be... onwards, it clarifies the ruin and destruction of the state.
Regarding the second section, which clarifies that propagating the sutra leads to the attainment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are four parts:
first, clarifying that the human king desires the peace and security of his realm;
second, from the passage beginning "This human king," etc., clarifying the exhortation for the human king to propagate the sutra.
From "We, the Four Kings... onwards, it clarifies the benefits obtained by the Four Kings.
From "As for the Brahmā deities... onwards, it clarifies the peace and security of the nation.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, it clarifies that the utility of this sutra surpasses those of the three treatises;
second, from the passage "Such immeasurable merits as these" onwards, it clarifies that the person who expounds this sutra surpasses the persons who expound those treatises.
Third, from the passage beginning "If in Jambudvīpa" onwards, it clarifies that the principles of this scripture surpass those of the three aforementioned treatises.
As for the term "Discourse on Transcending Desire," it refers to the four Vedas, which clarify matters such as Brahmā’s transcendence of desire.
What is called the "Discourse on Śakra" refers to the Kāraṇa-śāstra, which elucidates matters such as the ten wholesome actions.
What is called the "Discourse on the Immortals" refers to the Gārgya-śāstra, which elucidates matters such as the elixirs of the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā).

Why is this teaching superior to the other three treatises? Because this sutra, through the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata, extensively benefits all sentient beings by bestowing happiness and extracting them from suffering; therefore, it surpasses those other treatises.
"The power of great compassion surpasses that of Brahmā, and the power of ascetic practice surpasses that of Śakra" refers to citing one aspect from each side.
The second part, the description of the intermediate section, has two sub-sections:
first, the description of protecting the human king; second, from "If there is anyone who can... onwards, the description of protecting the masses. The textual structure of these passages is clear.
From "Having spoken the verses" onwards is the second major section, the Praise.
This contains two parts:
first, the four kings praise the Buddha; second, the Tathāgata praises the sutra.
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts:
first, the two initial lines that state the heading; second, the six lines of verse that offer praise; and third, the two lines that provide the conclusion.
Regarding the second [section], there are two parts:
The first four and a half lines praise the two bodies of response and transformation, while the final one and a half lines extol the dharma-body.
Within the former section, there are two parts:
the first three lines provide a brief summary, and the subsequent one and a half lines offer a detailed exposition.
The summary consists of two parts:
first, one and a half lines praise the physical form, radiance, countenance, and white teeth of the *nirmāṇakāya*; second, one and a half lines praise the merits of the body, wisdom, and samādhi.
The detailed explanation has two parts:
first, one line elaborates on the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body); second, half a line elaborates on the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
Within the praise of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body), the first half-line praises the essence of the *dharmakāya*, and the subsequent line praises its function.
Regarding the second section, the praise by the Tathāgata, there are four parts:
first, five lines of verse praising the great power of the sutra;
second, from "Within Jambudvīpa" onwards, twelve and a half lines of verse exhorting the human king to propagate it.
Third, from "This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*" down to four lines, it causes the celestial kings to provide protection;
fourth, from "If there be those who hear" down to three lines, it concludes the three preceding meanings.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
the first two verses praise the essence, and the subsequent three verses praise the function.
Within the first part, one verse clarifies the Dharma and the next verse clarifies the person.
Regarding the application [of these verses], the first line brings happiness, the next line generates goodness, and the final line uproots suffering.
Within the second major section, there are two parts among the twelve and a half lines:
the first four and a half lines exhort the propagation [of the teaching].
The eighteen lines beginning from "This sutra can act as... clarify the attainment of benefits.
Within the context of propagation, the first two and a half lines clarify the benefits for the propagator, while the final two lines provide the actual exhortation.
Regarding the two types of benefits obtained, there are two sections;
the first consists of one and a half verses of Dharma-exposition, which has three parts:
the first half-verse clarifies the arising of the goodness of the path, the next verse uproots the suffering of birth and death, and the final verse bestows the peace and happiness of the cause.
The second analogy has three parts:
first, the jewel tree; second, the cool water; and lastly, the precious jewels.
The meaning of the textual passages is clear.
Within the protection of the third day, there are four sections:
first, one line describes the offerings of the various devas; second, one line clarifies the protective maintenance of the Four Heavenly Kings—these two concern the True Dharma.
Third, one line describes the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas; fourth, one line clarifies the guardianship of ghosts and spirits—these two concern the protection of persons.
Regarding the fourth major section, the conclusion of the three preceding meanings consists of three parts:

first, one line concludes the first point, praising the greatness of the sutra’s power; second, one line concludes the second point, that human kings receive and uphold it; and third, one line concludes the third point, that celestial kings provide protection.

The prose following the verse constitutes the third major section, clarifying the joy felt upon hearing the sutra, the offering of scattered flowers, and the vow to protect those who propagate the sutra.
The phrase "the dharma of quiescence" (śāntadharma) refers to the essence of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) mentioned above.
*Mahāprajñāparivarta*: The following four chapters constitute the second major section, clarifying the category of persons—those who benefit and propagate [the teaching].
This is further divided into four parts:
the first chapter, "Bestowing Merit," benefits material resources; the "Earth Deity Chapter" provides food and drink; and the "Vajrapāṇi Chapter" benefits wisdom.
If one lacks eloquence (*pratibhāna*), the necessities of life such as clothing and food, and wisdom, one cannot propagate the Dharma; therefore, these four deities successively provide for them.

This Great Eloquence Deity (*Mahāpratibhāna*) has his traces in the heavens; as the deity is originally a Bodhisattva of the ninth stage (*navamī bhūmi*) who is fully endowed with the four types of eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), it is called the "Chapter on Great Eloquence."
The text consists of two parts:
first, the discourse on benefiting those who speak;
second, from "He shall cause these [beings]... onwards, the discourse on benefiting the audience.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, the explicit clarification of the benefits for the speaker;
second, from the passage beginning "If there are sentient beings... onwards, the exhortation to speak it for others.
Furthermore, regarding the first [section], there are two parts:

first, it augments the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The first three phrases augment the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*); the next two phrases augment the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); and the final phrase collectively clarifies the two analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dharma*) and meaning (*artha*).
Second, from the passage "If, within this sutra... onwards, it augments the power of dhāraṇī.

In the second section, which exhorts one to speak for others, the first part identifies those to be converted as possessing roots of goodness; the second part, beginning from "This Dharma-preacher," correctly exhorts one to speak for others.
The second major section, "Benefiting the Audience," has three parts:
first, benefiting their merit and wisdom—initially bestowing wisdom and subsequently benefiting their meritorious retribution;

second, from the phrase "excellent words" (*suvākya*) downward, bestowing the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): "skillfully understanding expedient means" refers to the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*); "being well able to expound various treatises" refers to the analytical knowledge of joyful speech (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); and "skillfully knowing technical arts" refers to the two analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) and meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
The third section, from "Able to transcend birth and death" onwards, clarifies the attainment of the Buddha-fruit.
*Chapter on the Goddess Guṇakāra*: This deity resides among the kings of tree-spirits; she is named "Merit" (*Guṇa*) because wherever she goes, she bestows supreme bliss upon others.
In foreign lands, gods are also called *devas*.
These gods originally belong to the first stage (*bhūmi*); since the first stage is fully endowed with the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), they possess sovereign mastery over material wealth.
There are two categories:
first, that which is required by the speaker;
second, from the passage "I have already passed away" onwards, that which is given as material wealth to the audience.
In this chapter, one also provides food and drink, yet providing material wealth is primary.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, the actual provision of what is needed, up to enabling them to seek out the sūtras.
The second section, from "If there are sentient beings... onwards, exhorts the propagation of the sutra.

Within this, the first part clarifies the roots of goodness of those to be converted; the section beginning with "This Dharma-preacher... properly exhorts the propagation; and the section beginning with "These sentient beings... clarifies the benefits for those to be converted.
The second major section concerns giving material wealth to listeners;
it contains two parts:
first, explaining the virtue of having something to give.
The second section, beginning with "If there is anyone who can," correctly explains the granting of what is required.

Within this, first it clarifies the planting of roots of goodness in past lives; then, from "Therefore, I now" onwards, it clarifies that in this present life one has obtained retribution according to one's wishes, such that one is able—by means of a compassionate mind following wherever one thinks, by means of the divine eye following wherever one looks, and by means of supernormal powers following wherever one goes—to cause sentient beings to experience happiness and to be fully endowed with the seven treasures.
Regarding the second major section, there are three parts to what is required:

first, a brief explanation; second, a detailed exposition beginning from "In this northern direction" below; and third, a concluding exhortation beginning from "One should with a sincere heart" below.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts.
First is the clarification of causing them to cultivate the causes.

As for cultivating the causes, this refers to invoking the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, making offerings to the Buddhas as Guṇakārandavatī, and separately offering incense and flowers to the celestial deities.
Second, from the passage "One should know that this person" onwards, it clarifies the attainment of the fruit.
As for the attainment of the fruit, it refers to the flourishing and production of all things, such as wealth, treasures, the essence of the earth, grains, and fruits.
The second section also has two parts:
first, the exhortation to cultivate the cause;
second, from "From this day and night" onwards, the clarification of attaining the fruit.
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts:
first, indicating the location;
second, from "If there are those who wish to attain... onwards, the actual exhortation to cultivate the causes.
From the section beginning with "Making this vow" downward, the future life is clarified.
The first part is easily understood.
Regarding the second, within the cultivation of causes, there are four [sections]:
First, the purification of the internal and external: cleaning and sweeping the dwelling place is the external; donning robes and anointing the body is the internal.
Second, from "For my sake, with a sincere heart" onwards, it clarifies the making of offerings to the Triple Gem.
Third, from "At that time, one should speak" onwards, it clarifies the recitation of mantras.
From "seven days and seven nights" onwards, the text clarifies the practice of making vows.
As for the term "mantra of consecration," it refers to what is known as a divine spell (*vidyā-mantra*).
There are generally four types of what is expounded by divine mantras:

first, praising the merits of the Buddhas; second, explaining the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); third, clarifying medicinal herbs; and fourth, chanting the names of spirits and deities. That which is elucidated here should be the merits of the Buddhas.
It clarifies the merits of all Buddhas, anoints the crowns of sentient beings’ faith, and causes them to ascend the throne of the Dharma King.
It is named "Anointment" (Abhiṣeka) because it is designated by way of analogy;
it is called "Auspicious and Not in Vain" because one will certainly obtain wholesome fruits through the power of this mantra.
Regarding "sentient beings of equal conduct," those who wish to practice this dharma must have companions of similar conduct.

Regarding "those with middling roots of goodness," this means that those with inferior faculties have hearts so thin that they cannot obtain the power of the mantra through recitation, while those with superior faculties possess such profound virtue that they do not rely on the power of the mantra; therefore, one must necessarily possess middling faculties.
The fourth [section], on the practice of making vows, is easy to understand.
Regarding the third [section], on the arrival of the devas: the initial part instructs one to arouse mindfulness;
from the passage "In one's own dwelling" onwards, it clarifies the purification of the residence to await their arrival.
From the passage beginning "At that time, I... onwards, it clarifies the arrival of the celestial deity.
Within the second major section, "Attaining the Fruit," this first part clarifies that there was no need to beg for what was required; this constitutes the bestowing of happiness.
From the passage beginning with "If one can, by means of oneself... onwards, it clarifies the protection and assistance provided from beginning to end; this is the removal of suffering.
The second section, the summary exhortation, is easily understood.

The "Chapter on the Firm and Steadfast Earth Deity" (*Sthira-pṛthivī-devatā-parivarta*): This chapter is the third [section] concerning the benefits for the practitioner through the gift of food and drink.
This deity is able to sustain the earth so that it does not perish, and thus receives its title based on this merit.

This deity is a manifestation of an earth deity (*pṛthivī-devatā*), yet its original nature is that of a bodhisattva from the first bhūmi (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward; therefore, it possesses the sovereign power to bestow food and drink.
This chapter consists of three sections:
first, it clarifies how the earth deities make offerings to those who propagate the sutra;
second, from the passage beginning with "At that time," it clarifies how, by virtue of making such offerings, one attains the ability to propagate the sutra.
Third, from the passage "These sentient beings, each in their respective dwellings" onwards, it clarifies that by means of propagation one attains superior fruits.
Regarding this first section, there are three parts;
the first indicates the location.
Second, from "The World-Honored One followed this sutra" onwards, the actual offering is clearly explained;
third, from "After I had heard the Dharma" onwards, the benefits gained from hearing the Dharma are clarified.
The first two [points] are easy to understand.
Regarding the third, there are two parts:
first, explaining how the earth deities obtain benefit; [the second follows].
Second, from the passage beginning "And this great earth," it clarifies how sentient beings obtain benefits.
This section contains three parts:

first, it clarifies that by reciting [the mantra], the essence of the earth emerges, increasing the hundred flavors and providing nourishment for physical strength and a particularly wondrous complexion; this constitutes material benefit.
Second, from "Accomplishing such as this" onwards, the benefits of the Dharma are clarified.
Third, from "Therefore, in the world" onwards, the conclusion is made.

First, the conclusion regarding material wealth is reached; from "All these sentient beings" onwards, the conclusion regarding the benefits of the Dharma is reached, the meaning of which is clear from the textual context.
In the second major section, which elucidates the propagation of the sutra, there are three parts:
first, the earth deity’s request for the preaching of this sutra;
second, from the words "For what reason" onwards, the elucidation of how the preaching of the sutra benefits sentient beings.
Third: From "Therefore, World-Honored One" onwards, the text exhorts people to listen and receive [the teaching].
The first two parts are easily understood.
Within the third part, the initial section clarifies the instruction for mindfulness;
Second, from "I shall certainly... onwards, it clarifies the exhortation to listen and receive;

third, from "Having already listened and received... onwards, it clarifies the self-congratulation for possessing five matters: first, congratulating oneself on hearing the Dharma; second, from "Already having been taken up... onwards, congratulating oneself on the acquisition of merit; third, from "Having encountered... onwards, congratulating oneself on encountering the Buddhas; fourth, from "The three evil [realms]... onwards, congratulating oneself on escaping the miserable destinies; and fifth, from "In future lives... onwards, congratulating oneself on being born among humans and devas.
Regarding the third major section, which clarifies the attainment of fruits through the propagation of the sutra, there are three parts:
first, the earth goddess clearly elucidates the attainment of the fruit; second, the Tathāgata’s response and narration; and third, the earth goddess’s reverent recompense.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
the first clarifies the propagation of the sutra.
"A single analogy" refers to the presence of a single parable within the sutra.
Regarding "a single condition," the sūtra explains two matters: first, the matter of the vow as the single cause, and second, the matter of the conditions.
From the words "World-Honored One" onwards, it clarifies the attainment of the fruit.
"The earth is fertile and things flourish; sentient beings enjoy happiness" clarifies the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*).
"Abounding in wealth and goods" and below clarify the fruit of habituation (*niṣyandaphala*).
Within the second section, the Buddha’s description, there are two parts:
First, it clarifies that the listeners obtain retribution;
second, from "The Earth Deity" onwards, it clarifies that those who make offerings obtain retribution.
Within the second section, "Repaying with Gratitude," there are three parts:
First, it clarifies the earth deity’s offering to the speaker;
second, from "If there are sentient beings" onwards, it clarifies the hearing by sentient beings;

third, from "These sentient beings" onwards, it clarifies the fruits obtained by sentient beings, first clarifying the reception of joyful retribution, and second, from "Encountering" onwards, clarifying the attainment of the fruit.
The textual characteristics are clear and distinct; there is no need for a prolix explanation.
The "Chapter on the Kumbhāṇḍa Spirit Vajrapāṇi" constitutes the fourth major section, clarifying the bestowal of wisdom.
In foreign lands he is called Saṃjñeya-sumati, which here is translated as "Secret Deity" (Mishen).
His traces appear as a king of ghosts, yet his original nature is that of a tenth-stage bodhisattva; thus, by means of the power of his wisdom, he is able to benefit those who propagate the sutras.
This section consists of three parts:
first, clarifying those who benefit from propagating the sutra;
second, from "For this reason" onwards, clarifying that the speaker gains benefits and is thus able to propagate the sutra.
Third, from "Namo" [homage] onwards, one takes refuge in the multitude of sages.
Because of the power of taking refuge in the multitude of sages, the aforementioned two capacities are attained.
Regarding the first [of these two], there are two parts:
First, it clarifies the protection through supernatural power that eliminates evil;
second, from the passage beginning with "For what reason and cause," it correctly clarifies how the power of wisdom increases the eloquence of the speaker.
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts:
first, clarifying the person who provides protection;
second, from "This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*... onwards, clarifying the Dharma that is protected.
From "I shall, by means of this" onwards, the text correctly elucidates the matter of protection.
Within this, first is the protection of the speaker, next the protection of the audience, and finally the protection of the land; the structure of the text is easily understood.
The second major section contains two parts:
first, an explanation of the virtues that provide benefit;

second, from "World-Honored One, General Vajrapāṇi" onwards, the actual explanation of the three ways of benefiting beings, which consists of: first, a summary indication; second, an explanation starting from "I know"; and third, a conclusion starting from "For this reason."
Within the second explanation, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the virtue of being able to know the two truths;
second, from the phrase "I see directly" onwards, clarifying the virtue of possessing the two wisdoms that can know [them].
Third, from the passage "I [regard] all dharmas" onwards, the two preceding points are concluded together. Regarding the two truths, each possesses both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*):

the differentiation of delusive phenomena is the phenomenon of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the provisional nature of dependent origination is the principle of conventional truth; the true phenomena as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are the phenomenon of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and those sands themselves being thus is the principle of ultimate truth.
"I know all phenomena" refers to knowing the matters of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"All conditioned phenomena" refers to the principle of conventional truth.
The first two characters, "I know," pervade and connect through the following two phrases.

Regarding "comprehending all dharmas and knowing the limits of dharmas": this is a reiterative clarification of the illumination concerning the knowledge of the limits of dharmas; thus, by saying "comprehending all dharmas," it clarifies the first phrase.

Knowing that the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) have the provisional and the illusory as their defining limit, it says "the defining limit of phenomena" (*dharma-pramāṇa*), which clarifies the subsequent phrase.
"The suchness-nature of all phenomena" refers to the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Principle has no duality, and is therefore called "Suchness" (*tathatā*);
that which does not change is called "nature" (*prakṛti*), and this "nature" is also its essence (*svabhāva*).
That which contains all phenomena within all phenomena refers to the reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Within each individual virtue, all virtues are subsumed; therefore, it is said that they "contain and receive" them.
The first four characters, "abiding in accordance with the Dharma," pervade through the following two phrases.
Realizing according to principle and knowing according to phenomena, there is no effortful movement of the mind; therefore, it is said that one dwells in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding the second [section], which clearly elucidates the two types of knowledge: the first four lines clarify the essence of the knowledge of clarity, while the final line clarifies the function of the knowledge of clarity.
The term "Wisdom-Light" (*jñānaprabhā*) clarifies true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*);
it illuminates according to the dharma without any obscuration, like the light of the sun.
The term "Wisdom-Torch" (*jñānolkā*) clarifies skillful means wisdom (*upāyajñāna*); it illuminates in accordance with conditions, like the brightness of a torch.
Regarding the term "practice of wisdom" (*jñāna-caryā*), it clarifies that the latter two types of wisdom do not constitute practice; rather, they are the practice itself.
Regarding "accumulation of wisdom" (*jñāna-rāśi*), it refers to the accumulation of manifold virtues within the former two types of wisdom; therefore, it is called an "accumulation."
The essence of clear wisdom is concluded.

Regarding the term "object of wisdom," it refers to the objects manifested by the two aforementioned types of wisdom; because they are like transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), they are called "objects."
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The realms of all Buddhas are entirely impermanent.

This essence of wisdom and its function are both nameless and signless; because they are signless, they cannot be conceived, and because they are nameless, they cannot be discussed—hence, they are called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
The King of Ghosts bears witness that these are not illusory mental objects or appearances; therefore, he says, "I see them manifest.

Within the third section on "Correct Understanding," "correct understanding" refers to knowing that the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are not erroneous; hence, it is called correct understanding.
Since this is not an inference (*anumāna*), it is called "correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*).
Since it is not a cognition of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), it is termed "correct discernment" (*samyag-vikalpa*).
This concludes the aforementioned knowledge of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Correctly understanding conditions" concludes the aforementioned knowledge of the principles of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

"Correctly awakening and comprehending" is a general summary of the knowledge of the phenomena and principles of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), as well as the essence of wisdom, the function of wisdom, and their respective objects.
In the second major section, which correctly elucidates the benefiting of sentient beings, there are two parts:
first, the elucidation of the beneficial activities, namely the fulfillment of five things—eloquence, physical strength, valor, wisdom, and mindfulness;
second, from the phrase "the mind is without... onwards, the manifestation of the characteristics of benefit, namely the three things of being untiring, experiencing joy, and feeling gladness.
In the second major section, which clarifies how the speaker benefits from being able to propagate the sutra, there are four parts:
first, it clarifies that the speaker possesses the wisdom to preach;
second, from the passage beginning "If there are sentient beings... onwards, it clarifies that the listeners possess the goodness and capacity to receive [the teaching].
3. From "the person who preaches the Dharma" onwards, it clarifies the exhortation to preach for the sake of sentient beings, thereby fulfilling the first point;

4. From "immeasurable sentient beings" onwards, it clarifies the benefits gained by the listeners—namely, the five kinds of benefit consisting of wisdom, merit, the experience of happiness, bodhi, and the departure from suffering.
The third major section, on taking refuge, is easily understood.
From here on, the seven chapters constitute the second major section, elucidating how those who propagate this sutra obtain its power.
Within this, there are two parts:
the first three chapters explain the benefits of the causes obtained by those who propagate [the teaching], while the latter four chapters clarify the benefits of the fruits obtained.
Regarding the first three chapters, they are further divided into three sections:

First, in the "Chapter on the Correct Discourse," the manifestation of the marks of clarity and their extensive proclamation are elucidated; next, in the "Chapter on the Good Collection," the extensive proclamation of Śākyamuni is elucidated; and finally, in the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits," the extensive proclamation by the fourfold assembly is elucidated.

Regarding the term "Righteous Discourse" (Saddharma-vyākaraṇa): it refers to the dialogue between the Four Heavenly Kings and Brahmā, which clarifies the righteous Dharma for governing and transforming [the world]; therefore, it is named the "Chapter on Righteous Discourse.
A question is raised:
Since the righteous Dharma for governing a nation is a worldly discourse, how can it be called the propagation of this sutra that yields causal benefits?
The commentary states:

The virtue of transformative governance is precisely the wisdom and great compassion of an impartial mind; were it not for relying on the sutras to practice, by what means could one attain this impartial governance that makes no distinction between enemy and kin?
This chapter has two parts:
first, an explanation of dependent origination;
second, from the section beginning with "What is... onwards, the formal exposition of the dependent origination of the correct teaching, which is easy to understand.
Regarding the second [section], the first part indicates the commencement; from the verse onward is the actual exposition of the treatise.
Within this, there are three parts:
the first two lines of verse provide the admonition and the promise.
Second, from "The kings gather together" downward, there are four verses of inquiry;
third, from "The Four World-Protecting Kings" downward, there are seventy-six verses of explanation.
Regarding the "exhortation and permission," this refers to the Father King’s entrustment to Prince Śraddhālakṣa to expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Within the second section, the "questions and requests," there are two parts:
the first two lines clarify the praise and request of the Four Heavenly Kings, while the subsequent two lines of verse set forth the specific matters of their request.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, one line of inquiry; second, one line of verse as a conclusion.
Regarding the inquiry, there are three matters:
The first two phrases ask why this person is called a "deva" (heavenly being);
the next phrase asks why this person alone is called a "king";
and the final phrase asks why a human king is called a "son of heaven" (*devaputra*).
The final line provides a summary.
It asks:
although they dwell among humans, are they called "devas" (heavenly beings) because they govern the world with the True Dharma?
This concludes the first question.
The second and third are omitted without being formally concluded.
Within the explanation of the second [question], there are two parts:
The first two and a half lines grant permission to speak;
the second part, from "Because of the accumulation of karma" (*hetu-samudaya-karma*) downward, consists of seventy-three and a half lines that constitute the formal response.
Within this, there are two sections:
The first six lines provide a brief answer concerning the essence of the correct treatise;

the second section, from "Half [of this] is called the King of Men" downward, consists of sixty-seven and a half lines that provide an extensive answer revealing the characteristics of the correct treatise.
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts.
The first line answers the second question:
it states that although they are equally human beings, because he governs the land, he is called a king.
The second section, from "while dwelling in the womb" down to three and a half lines, answers the third question.
Within this, the first two lines clarify that while in the womb he was protected by devas; therefore, he is called a "Son of Heaven" (devaputra).
The next line clarifies that he is nurtured by the devas outside the womb; therefore, he is called a "Son of Heaven" (devaputra).
The subsequent line clarifies that after reaching adulthood, he is bestowed with a portion of the deva's virtue; therefore, he is called a "Son of Heaven."
The latter half of the verse is the conclusion.
Because he is empowered by the power of the devas, he attains mastery; thus, he is called a "deva.
From the line beginning with "distant from unwholesome dharmas" for one and a half lines, he provides a retrospective answer to the first question.
Within this, there are three parts:
the first half-verse clarifies that evil is extinguished by means of the celestial law, and thus it is called "heaven" (*deva*).
The latter half-verse clarifies that goodness is produced by means of the celestial law, and thus it is called "making one be born in heaven" as "heaven."
The latter half of the verse clarifies that one is born in the heavens by means of celestial laws; therefore, they are called "heavens.
The section beginning with "Half are named human kings" constitutes the second major section, which provides an extensive response.
Within this, there are two parts:
the first three stanzas extensively treat the virtue of transforming others;
the second part, from "If there are evil matters" onwards, consists of sixty-four and a half stanzas that extensively treat the correct discourse on transformation.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
the first one and a half lines distinguish the virtues based on the names;
the subsequent one and a half lines resolve doubts to manifest those virtues.
Regarding the term "half-human king": it is called "half" because one side is designated as a deva and the other side is designated as a human;
thus, these two together constitute the pair known as "human-deva."
They are also called "Musicians" (Gandharvas), for they uphold the rites and music of the world to transform people and bring them peace and happiness;
thus they are named "Musicians. They are also called "Rākṣasas," for those who commit evil feel fear toward the king; thus they are named "Rākṣasas."
These two are called the "pair that produces fear within those who seek pleasure.
Regarding the term "executioners" (kuài-huì): one who trades in fish and presides over butchering is called a *huì*, while one who trades in pigs and presides over butchering is called a *kuài*.
Because incantations eliminate evil and rectify what is improper for the ruler of the state, they are said to be able to ward off all evils.
They are called "parents" because they teach the cultivation of wholesome dharmas; therefore, they are named "parents."
This constitutes the pair of "restraining evil and teaching what is good.
Having completed the analysis of virtues based on their names, the following section is the second part: resolving doubts to manifest these virtues. Therein, there are two doubts:
The initial doubt asks: "If a human king is like a rākṣasa executioner who causes people to feel fear and dread, for what reason is he protected by the devas?
The explanation states:

A human king manifests the commission of evil so that there may be retribution, thereby inducing flogging and punishment to cause him fear and ensure he harbors no further malicious intent. Because he is thus protected by the devas, it is said that he manifests the fruits of retribution while being guarded by all the devas.
The section beginning with "the various karmas of good and evil" explains the second doubt.
The doubt asks: if sufferings such as flogging serve only to induce fear, then how is this present suffering obtained without a cause?
The commentary states:

Since the fruits of good and evil karma pertain to both the present and the future, sufferings such as flogging and the like are retributions for suffering experienced in the present; they do not arise without cause.
The section beginning with "If there are evil deeds" constitutes the second major section, which extensively explains the transformation through the True Dharma.
Within this, there are three sections:
the first thirty-five lines clarify that if a king of men indulges in evil, calamity arises and the state perishes;

the second, from "If he is one born under the protection of the various devas" onwards, consists of twenty-one and a half lines and clarifies that if a king of men cultivates goodness, blessings arrive and the land becomes abundant.
The third section, from "For this reason" (*etena hetunā*) downward, consists of eight lines and serves as a conclusion to exhort the abandonment of evil and the following of good.
Within this, there are four parts;
first, six and a half lines clarify how the people give rise to evil.
The second section, from "A violent wind suddenly arises" for twelve and a half lines, clarifies the arising of evil by the sovereign;
the third section, from "Those who receive favors and emoluments" for thirteen stanzas, clarifies the arising of evil by the ministers;
and the fourth section, from "If there is a king" for three lines of verse, provides a summary that all [evils] stem from the king.

Regarding the first section, the first two verses clarify the causes for committing evil; the next three verses clarify the attainment of the fruits of suffering; and the final one and a half verses conclude that such actions should not be performed—the textual structure is clear.
Regarding the commission of evil by a human king, there are also three parts:

first, one and a half lines clarify the attainment of the fruit of suffering—namely, the three types of results consisting of irregular winds and rains, the loss of the proper course of the stars and constellations, and the failure of fruits to ripen;
second, from "Because the king abandons what is right" downward, three lines of verse clarify the causes for committing evil.
The eight verses beginning with "Because of the gods' anger" extensively clarify the evil fruits [of such actions].
Among them, the first half-verse generally clarifies the ruin of the state;

the subsequent seven and a half lines specifically clarify the evil fruits, namely: illness, the ruin of the state, the separation from one's kin, calamities, strange portents, evil bandits, death by starvation, the loss of legitimate wealth, and the deviation of the constellations from their courses.
Regarding the third minister’s commission of evil, there are three parts:
first, one verse on the minister’s practice of unrighteousness;
second, two verses from "Thus practicing evil" onwards, clarifying the king's acquiescence.

Regarding "the one who grants permission": this refers to how a wicked minister receives the king’s singular favor and respect, while even when a virtuous minister declines and perishes, he is not even taken into account.
From the ten lines beginning with "Therefore, the three calamities arise simultaneously in the world" onwards, it clarifies the attainment of retribution as suffering.
Within this, the first two lines open the chapter’s topical outline (*uddāna*), while the subsequent eight lines provide the explanation.
Regarding the former, there are again two parts:
the first line clarifies the attainment of the characteristics of evil.
Regarding "evil signs," three anomalies arise simultaneously.
These three anomalies refer to the stars deviating from their courses, violent winds, and malignant rains.
The following line clarifies that there will be evil results.

As for the "evil fruits," these refer to the destruction of the supramundane True Dharma, the correct retribution of worldly sentient beings, and the "fertility of the earth" as their environmental support (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*).
Regarding the commentary, there are three parts:
the first half-verse cites the evil causes.
The second section, from "Therefore, heaven sends down hail" downward for six and a half lines, correctly explains the attainment of the results.

As for these results: they consist of death from hunger caused by hail, the withering and destruction of grain and fruit, the prevalence of illness throughout the land, and the reduction of sweet fruits while the bitter flavors increase.
Next, from "The Original Places of Play" onwards is the extensive explanation, which is understandable.
Third, from "There are many sufferings of illness" onwards, one line constitutes the conclusion.
From the passage beginning with "If there is a king" onwards is the fourth section, clarifying that all [consequences] stem from the king.
Within this, there are three parts:
the first line clarifies how the king causes his subjects to commit evil.
The following two lines clarify that they are made to suffer;
the subsequent one and a half lines correctly clarify that it is entirely due to the king.

From the passage beginning with "If for the sake of the devas" onwards is the second major section, clarifying that when a king of men cultivates goodness, blessings arrive and the land becomes abundant.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, one and a half lines clarify that if the king does not commit evil, the people will practice goodness and be reborn in the heavens.
Second, from "Those who practice unwholesome deeds" down to two and a half lines, it clarifies that the people suffer for committing evil because the king permits wickedness and fails to punish it;
third, from "Arising of all manner of treachery and evil" down to seventeen and a half lines, it clarifies that when the king governs justly, the kingdom immediately attains abundance and joy.
The first two [sections] are easy to understand.
Regarding the third, there are three parts:
the first five and a half lines provide a general admonition against evil and an exhortation toward good;
Second, from "One should not commit evil" downward for four lines, it specifically clarifies that the state perishes through the commission of evil;
third, from "Transforming the state with goodness" downward for eight lines, it specifically clarifies that the land prospers through the practice of goodness.
Next, the eight lines beginning with "For this reason" constitute the third major section, which clarifies the exhortation to abandon evil and follow good.
The textual structure is clear; there is no need for a laborious explanation.
The "Chapter on the Good Collection" (*Susaṃbhava-parivarta*): "Good Collection" (*Susaṃbhava*) is Śākyamuni himself, and "Jeweled Profundity" (*Ratnaguhya*) is Akṣobhya himself.
Since this chapter primarily elucidates the affairs of King Susaṃbhava, it is named accordingly.
This chapter consists of two parts:
first, the prose exposition; second, the explanation by means of verses.
Within the verses, there are two sections:
The first fifty-one and a half lines clarify the cause;
the second section, from "At that time, the bhikṣu who preached the Dharma for the king" onwards, consists of twelve and a half lines and clarifies the attainment of the fruit.
Regarding the causes for practice, there are two parts:
first, the initial four lines clarify the practice of giving;
second, from "Furthermore, in past lives" onwards, forty-seven and a half lines clarify the practice of wisdom.
There are four types of the practice of giving:
the first line concerns the relinquishing of kingdoms and cities;
the next line concerns the relinquishing of precious treasures.
The next line concerns abandoning one's retinue;
the next line concerns abandoning body and life.
Within the third section, "Attaining Wisdom," there are two parts:
The first eighteen lines clarify the causes and conditions for seeking the Dharma;
the second section, from "At that time, the Honored One Ratnagarbha" downward, consists of twenty-nine and a half lines and constitutes the actual hearing of the Dharma.
Within this, there are four sections:
first, the eleven lines clarify the acceptance of the invitation;
second, from "At that time, Ratnākara" downward, the eight lines constitute the actual preaching of the sutra.
3. From "At that time, the Great King" downward for two and a half lines, it clarifies the joy of hearing the Dharma;
4. From "Desiring to make offerings" downward for eight lines, it clarifies the offering made as a repayment of kindness.
Regarding the third section, "Attaining Fruition through the Teaching of the Dharma," there are three parts:
first, the two initial verses, which correlate the ancient and the present;

second, the eight and a half lines beginning with "At that time," which clarify the attainment of fruition; and third, the three lines beginning with "The merit thus obtained," which collectively conclude the discussion on cause and effect.

〈Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits〉: This chapter clarifies that when the fourfold assembly listens to and receives [the teaching], they will possess superior goodness and be protected by ghosts and spirits; therefore, it is named after them.
This chapter consists of three sections:
first, from the beginning of the chapter to the twenty-sixth verse, there is the exhortation for the assembly to listen and receive [the teaching];

second, from "The Great Brahma King" downward to forty-eight and a half lines, there is the clarification of the protection provided by the eight classes of beings; [and third, the remaining portion].
The third section, from "This sutra" onwards, consists of twenty-seven and a half lines and clarifies the possession of all supreme fruits.
Within this initial part, there are two sections:
first, the prose passage and the following two lines of verse, which directly exhort one to listen and receive [the teaching].
Second, from the verse "This wondrous sūtra" onwards, there are twenty-four lines of verse praising the great power of the sūtra.
This section consists of two parts:
the prose and the verse.

In the prose section, first the merit of making offerings to all Buddhas is presented; next, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) practiced by the Buddhas of Wisdom is presented; finally, it exhorts: "If you wish to attain the aforementioned merit and wisdom, you should listen to this sutra."
The verses can be understood [as follows].
Regarding the second section, which praises the power of the sutra, there are two parts:
first, nine lines of verse that directly praise the power of the sutra; [the rest follows].
