Second, from the line "Wherever one goes" onwards, there are fifteen verses that praise the benefits to encourage listening.
This section consists of two parts:
the first two lines praise the power to uproot suffering; [the remainder praises the power to bestow happiness].
From the passage "This sutra is profound" onwards, there are seven lines that praise the generation of merit and wisdom.
Of these, the first line praises the power of the sutra, and the second line clarifies its extraction from suffering and affliction.
The second section also has two parts:
the first two and a half lines clarify the praise of the sutra’s virtues.
Regarding the phrase "good in the beginning, middle, and end," this clarifies that these three refer to ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
It may also be divided into three parts: the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Circulation.
The second section, from "If one enters this sutra" downward for four and a half lines, clarifies the generation of merit and wisdom.
Among these, the first two lines clarify the arising of wisdom.
"Entering the dharma-nature" clarifies the realization of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
"Attaining the vision of me" refers to seeing the two bodies: the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Next, two and a half lines clarify the arising of merit.
Regarding the second section, which exhorts one to listen by highlighting its benefits, there are two parts:
first, two lines that directly exhort one to endure hardships in order to listen and receive the teaching;
The thirteen lines beginning with "Because of hearing this sutra" clarify the benefits of hearing the sutra.
This section contains three parts:
first, one and a half lines clarify the characteristics of the eradication of evil by the listener.
The second section, consisting of five verses beginning from "In the place of preaching the Dharma," clarifies the superior signs obtained by the speaker.

Regarding these superior signs: it is said that even when descending from the Dharma seat to address the great assembly, one still perceives the physical forms and images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as other visual phenomena, upon that Dharma seat.
The phrase "no different from before" means that originally there was no such characteristic, and after its cessation, it is likewise non-existent as it was before.
From the third section, "accomplishing such," down to six and a half lines of verse, one is enabled to attain the supreme fruit.
Among these, the first four and a half lines correctly clarify the attainment of the supreme fruit.

Regarding the "supreme fruit," it refers internally to possessing the majestic power and renown praised by all Buddhas, and externally to defeating enemies, evil dreams, and evil karma, as well as entering battle and achieving victory over others.
Next, the two lines of verse beginning with "The fame spreads abroad" serve as the conclusion.
Within the second major section, which clarifies the protection by the eight classes of beings, there are four parts;
of these, four and a half lines clarify the offerings.
Second, from "giving rise to the inconceivable" below, five lines and a half clarify veneration;
third, from "such great compassion" below, four lines clarify praise;
fourth, from "such sentient beings" below, thirty-four lines and a half clarify protection.
The textual characteristics are evident.
From the verse beginning with "Those who [uphold] this sutra" downwards, these twenty-eight verses constitute the third major section, clarifying the possession of all supreme fruits.
Within this section, there are two parts. First, twenty-six lines specifically clarify eight matters. These eight matters are as follows:

the first line and phrase increase physical strength and beauty; the second two lines eliminate calamities and disasters; the third four lines bring forth the fertility of the earth; the fourth two lines produce happiness; the fifth three lines cause grains, fruits, and plants to grow; the sixth three lines and phrases produce beautiful flowers; the seventh and eighth lines provide benefit through the illumination of light; and the final two lines ensure that the yin and yang are harmoniously adjusted.
The final two lines of verse constitute the second summary.

In the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions," the first three chapters clarify the benefits of attaining the cause; from here on, the second major section—comprising four chapters—clarifies that those who propagate the sutra attain the fruit.
Within this section there are two parts:

the first chapter correctly clarifies the attainment of the fruit, while the subsequent three chapters clarify the meaning of attaining the fruit through the cultivation of causes based on specific conditions.

Although the preceding "Chapter on the Correct Discourse" and others have clarified those who attain the fruit, they did not clarify the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); therefore, this current chapter correctly clarifies the attainment of the prediction. Since the attainment of a prediction necessarily depends upon superior causes, [the following chapters explain them].
The final three chapters extensively demonstrate the meaning of attaining the prediction [of enlightenment] based on past causes.
"Bestowing" (授) means to give, and "prediction" (記) means to determine.
Because it involves the determination that one will attain the fruit of Buddhahood through the stage of faith and so forth, it is named the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions."
This chapter consists of four sections:
first, an explanation of the assembly gathered for the bestowal of predictions;

second, from the words "The Buddha said" onwards, the actual bestowal of predictions, which begins with the prediction concerning the marks of faith, followed by the prediction concerning the two sons, and finally the prediction concerning the various devas.
The third section, from "At that time, at the site of enlightenment" onwards, clarifies the doubts arising in the tree deity and consists of three parts:
first, a brief presentation; second, a detailed explanation from "World-Honored One" onwards; and third, a concluding request from "World-Honored One, you are a son of heaven" onwards.
The fourth section, from "At that time, the Buddha said" onwards, is the Tathāgata’s resolution of those doubts.
This section contains three parts: first, a brief presentation;
second, an explanation beginning from "Why is this so?"; and third, a conclusion beginning from "Therefore. Regarding "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*):

it is said that within the celestial son there exists the internal cause of practicing virtue, while externally there is the condition of the Tathāgata’s original vows; thus, they are called causes and conditions.
Furthermore, having generated the wholesome cause of a pure mind upon hearing the sutra, and by virtue of the condition of hearing the Great Being’s prophecy, he received his own prophecy.

"Cultivating according to characteristics" refers to the practices such as the six *pāramitās*; it means that this devaputra, in the past, cultivated and practiced these in accordance with conditions and characteristics.

〈Chapter on Healing Illnesses〉: From this point onward, these three chapters constitute the second major section, which clarifies the principle that by cultivating causes in the past, one achieves the attainment of the fruit; that is, it extensively explains the causes and conditions for bestowing predictions (vyākaraṇa) in order to dispel the aforementioned doubts.
Within this, there are two parts:
the first two chapters primarily establish the "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies" while incidentally clarifying the "Chapter on the Lifespan";
the subsequent "Chapter on Casting Off the Body" primarily establishes the "Chapter on the Lifespan" while incidentally establishing the "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies."

The first two chapters correctly clarify that the ten thousand devaputras assumed the bodies of fish; because this was the cause for hearing the Dharma, they have today attained the prediction [of enlightenment], and thus it is said that they have correctly received their prediction.

This indicates that Śākyamuni was once a householder who cultivated the practice of loving-kindness and compassion to attain Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that this "indirectly reveals" his lifespan.

The final chapter correctly clarifies that Śākyamuni was once a prince who cultivated the cause of great compassion and has now attained Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that this "directly reveals" his lifespan.
Since the Buddha attained the fruit by cultivating the causes, how could Xinxiang (Faith-Aspect) not likewise do so?
Therefore, it is said that this [chapter] corroborates the bestowal of the prediction from a collateral perspective.

Within these two chapters, this "Chapter on Healing Illnesses" clarifies the distant conditions for attaining the prediction, while the "Chapter on Flowing Water" clarifies the proximate conditions; the distinction between the near and the far may be sought therein.
This chapter elucidates how Śākyamuni, in a former life, healed illnesses through great compassion; therefore, it is titled "The Chapter on Healing Illnesses.
Within this chapter, there are two parts:
first, the admonition and the promise to speak.
The second section, from "From the past" onwards, clarifies the actual exposition.
This actual exposition has two parts:
first, the narration of the Jātaka;...
Second, from "At that time, within the kingdom" onwards, the primary narrative (nidāna) is elucidated.
This section consists of two parts:
first, it clarifies the time and place of the original birth; second... [the rest of the text follows].
Second, from "In this king’s realm" onwards, the actual account of the previous birth (jātaka) is clarified.
Within this second major section clarifying the past events (itivṛttaka), there are two parts:
from the beginning up to one and a half lines of prose following the verse, the essence of compassion is clarified;
Second, from "At that time, the son of the elder... onwards, the application of compassion is clarified.
This section consists of five parts;
the first clarifies that the people of the country were ill.
Second, from "The Virtuous Goddess" downward, it clarifies the contemplation of wishing to save;
third, from "At that time, the son of the elder" downward, it clarifies the inquiry into medical methods;
fourth, from "At that time, the father, the elder" downward, it clarifies the father's explanation for him.
The fifth section, from "The Goddess Bhadrayānī" onwards, clarifies the attainment of understanding through hearing the teaching.
The first two parts are easily understood.
Within the third part, the initial prose passage serves as the introduction, followed by four lines that constitute the formal inquiry.
There are four matters in the formal inquiry:

first, one line asks about the causes and conditions of the illness; second, one line asks about the diet during the illness; third, one line asks about the physician and medicine for the illness; and fourth, one line asks about the season.
Regarding the causes and conditions of illness: these consist of the four great elements, the five viscera, and the five conditions.

When the four great elements are disharmonious and the five viscera are injured or impaired, they cause disease in the various sense faculties; for example, when the liver is afflicted, there is eye disease, and when the kidneys are afflicted, there is deafness.
Regarding the causes of illness: sitting too much or sleeping too much gives rise to water-diseases; walking too much, leaning too much, or speaking too much gives rise to wind-diseases.
Furthermore, sitting too much gives rise to heat-diseases; excessive lust gives rise to all diseases, which are then classified as "equal-part" (sāṃnipātika) diseases.

Furthermore, when fire is deficient, phlegm and drink increase; if fire is excessive, heat increases; if wind is excessive, it fans the fire and increases the heat; and if water is excessive, phlegm increases and becomes cold.
There are six ways in which food and drink cause illness:
first, eating in excess;
second, eating too little.
Third, eating at improper times;
eating only when one is extremely hungry;
fourth, eating at improper times, being forced to eat even before one is hungry.
Fifth, food that causes obstruction, such as drinking raw milk after finishing a meal of meat;
sixth, eating what one has never eaten before by force, such as southerners drinking fermented grain-water or northerners drinking milk.
Furthermore, consuming ghee and honey in equal portions leads to death;
likewise, eating bitter herbs mixed with honey renders one impotent.
Both of these are obstructive foods.
Furthermore, if a person with a wind disorder (*vāta*) eats cold or damp flavors, it will shorten their lifespan;
if one with a heat disorder (*pitta*) drinks alcohol or eats wheat, raw beef, and the like, it will cause them to lose their eyesight and suffer from nosebleeds;
if one with a phlegm disorder (*śleṣman*) eats sweet, fatty, pungent, or sour foods, it will cause a runny nose, excessive secretions, diarrhea, and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "the fire of the body does not extinguish," it refers to the heat of illness following a full meal.
As for "not ceasing when one ought to cease," this is due to the presence of disease.
When water overflows and damages the lungs, it constitutes the disease of phlegm (*śleṣman*).
Regarding "medicines for treating diseases," there are four types of difficult-to-cure illnesses:
first, wind (*vāta*); second, phlegm; third, heat (*pitta*); and fourth, the combination of these factors (*sannipāta*).
Each of these four types has three grades:
first, those that can be cured; these are new illnesses where the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are still strong.
Second, those that are constantly treated but do not improve; these are cases where the four great elements have been excessively injured.
Third, there are those that cannot be cured, because they exhibit signs of certain death.
Regarding the categories of medicinal substances, they are as explained in the following text.

As for the "seasons of illness": from the fourth to the fifth month is the time when wind arises; the sixth and seventh months are the time when wind-related illnesses erupt; and the eighth and ninth months are the time when wind is extinguished.

Next, from the sixth and seventh months is the time when heat arises; from the eighth and ninth months is the time when heat emerges; and from the tenth month to the first month is the time when heat ceases.

Next, from the tenth month to the first month is the time when water arises; from the second and third months is the time when water-diseases emerge; and from the fourth month to the seventh month is the time when water-diseases cease.
Within the fourth major section of the response, there are two parts:
the first line is the Buddha’s introduction to his father’s reply, and the subsequent sixteen lines constitute the father’s actual reply.
Within this latter part, there are two further divisions:
The first three lines concern the duration for practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the latter thirteen lines constitute the actual method for curing illness.
Regarding the phrase "the three triads are fundamentally subsumed," there are two masters who provide interpretations.
The first interpretation states:
A year has four seasons, namely spring, summer, autumn, and winter; spring is the beginning of the seasonal cycle, and winter is its end.
Within each season there are three months, known as the first (máng), middle (zhòng), and last (jì).
The first month is early spring; the second month is mid-spring; the third month is late spring—the same applies to the subsequent three seasons.
The first month serves as the primary period, encompassing the following two months, all of which belong to the division of spring;
the fourth month serves as the primary period, encompassing the following two months, all of which belong to the division of summer.
The seventh month is the basis, encompassing the subsequent two months as entirely belonging to the autumnal period;
the tenth month is the basis, encompassing the subsequent two months as entirely belonging to the winter period.
Since each of the four seasons consists of three months, it is said that there are "three threes."
Yet it is said that the first month is taken as the basis, subsuming the subsequent three months; thus it is called "the three-months-by-three-month basis-subsumption.
This is a case of the basis subsuming the branches.
Furthermore, it says:
The first and second months are precisely the season of spring; wood reigns supreme therein, while earth is temporarily enshrined during the third month and is subsumed under spring.
The fourth and fifth months are precisely the season of summer; fire reigns supreme therein, while earth is temporarily enshrined during the sixth month and is subsumed under summer.
The seventh and eighth months are precisely the season of autumn; among them, metal reigns as sovereign, while earth is subsumed under autumn by virtue of its association with the ninth month.

The tenth and eleventh months are precisely the season of winter; among them, water reigns as sovereign, while earth is subsumed under winter by virtue of its association with the twelfth month (the *laba* month).

The soil supports the four seasons, taking the rectification of time as its foundation; since each of the three-month periods is subsumed within the central soil, it is said that "the threes are fundamentally subsumed.
This is a case of the host subsuming the guest, wherein the guest is the soil.
The second interpretation states:
According to the Buddha’s teachings, a year consists of three seasons—namely, winter, spring, and summer; winter is the beginning of the seasonal cycle, and summer is its end.
Each of the [remaining] seasons originally consists of four months, with the autumn season being omitted.
Within each of these three seasons, one month of autumn is subsumed; thus, there are four months within each season, which is why it is said that "the three [seasons] each originally subsume [one]."
The first "three" characters refer to the three months of autumn.
The subsequent "three original" characters refer to the three original months of winter, spring, and summer.
As for why, among the four seasons, the autumn season is specifically set aside, the explanation states:
there are generally two reasons.
First, it is to refute the attachment to the notion of permanence.
During the autumn season, people all take delight in maintaining their habitual routines; therefore, wishing to break through this attachment, the autumn season was abolished.
Second, the opening of the later *anvāroka* (rainy-season retreat) was established during the month of Kārttika.

The original name for *an-gu* (the summer retreat) was "summer sitting" (*xia-zuo*). If it were during the autumn season prior to the middle of the eighth month, it would instead become "autumn sitting"; therefore, it is appropriate to abolish [this practice].
Regarding the phrase "when two appear at once," there are also two interpretations.
The first interpretation states:

Within the four seasons, two months each constitute the primary periods; the earth is assigned to the four quarters, with each month and day categorized under yin and yang, thereby forming six seasons.

Regarding the six periods: the first and second months are when the King of Wood manifests; the fourth and fifth months are when the King of Fire manifests; the seventh and eighth months are when the King of Metal manifests; and the tenth and eleventh months are when the King of Water manifests.
The twelfth and third months are the periods when the yang-earth is temporarily sovereign; the sixth and ninth months are the periods when the yin-earth is temporarily sovereign.
Sovereignty is termed "manifestation" (*pratyupasthāna*); thus, it is said that with two manifestations each, the six periods are fully completed.
The second explanation states:
According to the three seasons of the Dharma, each season consists of four months, each of which has a first and a latter half, thus forming six periods. As for these six periods:
from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the second month, these two months constitute the first half of the spring season.
From the sixteenth day of the second month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month, these two months manifest as the latter part of spring.
From the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the sixth month, these two months manifest as the first part of summer;
from the sixteenth day of the sixth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month, these two months manifest as the latter part of summer.
From the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month, these two months manifest as the first part of winter;
from the sixteenth day of the tenth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, these two months manifest as the latter part of winter.
Therefore, it is said that if the two [factors] are each fully explained, they complete six periods.
Within the second section, the "Direct Response," there are two parts:
first, eleven and a half lines clarify the manifestation of illness according to the seasons; next, one and a half lines clarify illnesses provoked by the violation of seasonal timing.
Regarding the first section, there are seven parts:
the first line answers the second question above concerning illness and diet;
the next line answers the first question above concerning the causes and conditions of illness.
The third section, consisting of one and a half lines, answers the third question above regarding medicinal decoctions for illness;
the fourth section, consisting of two lines, answers the fourth question above regarding the timing of illness;
and the fifth section, consisting of two and a half lines, again answers the third question above regarding the medicine for treating illness.
The sixth two lines re-respond to the second question above regarding food and drink for the sick;
the seventh two and a half lines re-respond to the third question above regarding medicine for treating illness.

The reason why the question on medicine for treating illness is answered three times is as follows: the first section shows the prevention of illness with medicine before it occurs; the second section clarifies the treatment of illness with medicine once it has occurred; and the third section clarifies the restoration of health with medicine after the illness has been treated.

The reason for answering the second question twice is that the first part clarifies how food can sustain the body and prevent illness, while the latter clarifies how desire for food can damage the body and cause disease.

Regarding the phrase "as stated in medical prescriptions" in the first passage, it refers to the fact that within various medicinal formulas found in the *Bencao* (Pharmacopoeia), it is explained which foods are suitable and which are unsuitable; one must not rely on what is unsuitable.

Regarding the phrase "metabolic increase and decrease" mentioned in the second [section], it refers to the coming and going of the four seasons and the increase and decrease of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding the "six greats" mentioned in the third [section], these are the six viscera:
first, the large intestine; second, the small intestine; third, the spleen; fourth, the triple burner (*trijvālā*); and including the two lateral luminaries, they constitute six.
Regarding the statement in the fourth [section] that "wind disorders are active in summer," this is because in summer the pores open and communicate, allowing external wind to enter.
Regarding "fever disorders are active in autumn," this is because in autumn the pores are closed and obstructed, causing heat to remain latent within and unable to circulate.
Third, regarding "the equal distribution of winter-onset": when water is stirred during spring, lung diseases do not subside;
when heat is stirred during autumn, febrile diseases do not subside;
and when all [elements] are stirred during winter, it is because of all diseases.
Regarding the statement, "Lung diseases increase in spring," this is because the second and third lunar months are the time when diseases of phlegm and the two yin constituents arise.

Regarding the fifth [section], which states, "For wind diseases in summer, consume fatty and greasy foods," etc., it means that during the summer months the pores are open and dilated; therefore, it is appropriate to block them with fatty and greasy substances.
Salts are hot in nature and deplete water; they cause the body to become firm and solid, preventing wind from entering. Hot food induces sweating, through which wind is expelled.
Furthermore, they treat cold-natured vacuity, ensuring that wind cannot enter.
Cold and sweet substances, such as ghee and milk, are able to treat heat. Sweet, sour,
and fatty substances taken in winter in equal proportions— where the fat treats wind—
if one with a lung disease consumes fatty substances, it causes the pores to prevent water from entering.
Pungent and hot substances eliminate water; therefore, they can treat diseases of the lungs.

Regarding the statement in the sixth [section] that "overeating triggers lung disease": when one has eaten excessively until the intestines and stomach are fully distended, it consequently triggers lung disease.

Regarding "fever arises when digestion occurs": at the beginning, when one eats rotten *kustumburu* (a type of grain), fever arises again as the food is digested; later, because wind (*vāta*) gathers in the empty interior, wind-disease (*vātavyādhi*) arises.
In the seventh [chapter], it says "wind [is treated] with clarified butter and fats" (*sarpistaila*): because wind is thin and sparse, it is supplemented with fatty substances.
As the heat-energy has not yet subsided and one wishes to purge and treat the heart and abdomen, one therefore takes purgative medicine.
In cases where the humors are in equilibrium, one should treat wind with ghee and richness, remove heat with sweetness, and remove water with pungency.
Lung disease is characterized by water; one should take emetic medicine.
The next line and a half eliminate diseases caused by irregular timing; these should be managed according to the previous instructions.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, the son of a householder," begins the second major section.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, it clarifies that through kind words of consolation, a light illness is immediately cured;
as for those with serious illnesses, they are cured only when given medicine.
The third section is the "Combined Concluding Section.
The textual characteristics are evident.
In the "Chapter on the Elder’s Son Sudāna," this second part elucidates the proximate causes for the attainment of mindfulness.
It differs from the preceding three in two ways:
first, whereas the former generates loving-kindness toward beings of the same class—namely human beings—here one generates loving-kindness toward beings of a different class—namely animals;
second, whereas the former is the loving-kindness that treats physical illness, this is the loving-kindness that removes mental affliction.
Third, whereas the preceding section clarified mundane compassion (*laukika-maitrī*), this section clarifies supramundane compassion (*lokottara-maitrī*).
Because there are these three distinctions, this chapter is titled "The Near Cause for Receiving the Prediction" (*vyākaraṇa-upaniṣad*).
This chapter has three sections:
first, praising the virtue of removing illness; second, clarifying the merit of rescuing the fish; third, concluding by correlating the past with the present.
Within the first section, there are two parts:
The first part clarifies how the elder eliminates illness;
the second part, beginning from "Because the illness has been eliminated," clarifies how sentient beings cultivate merit and offer respectful praise as a way of repaying his kindness.
Within the second major section, there are also two parts:
first, the account of the elder saving the fish;
second, from the passage "intoxicated and lying down" onwards, the account of the ten thousand fish repaying his kindness.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, an explanation of the original life story (*jātaka*) of the husband and wife and their two sons;
second, from the passage "This elder’s son... onwards, an explanation of the events of that original life story.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the account of the elder seeing the fish and being taught by the tree deity to save them, whereby he gives rise to a mind of compassion—this clarifies the essence of compassion;
second, from the passage "At that time, in this empty pond" onwards, it clarifies the function of compassion.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of material giving (*āmiṣadāna*);
second, from "After giving food to the fish" onwards, the explanation of the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
Within the second major section on repaying kindness, there are three parts:
first, explaining rebirth in heaven;
second, from "At that time, ten thousand... onwards, explaining the repayment of kindness.
Third, from the passage "At that time in Jambudvīpa" onwards, it clarifies the awakening of the king;
the textual structure is evident.

In the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body," this chapter clarifies how Śākyamuni’s ascetic practices resulted in the fruit of his lifespan, while incidentally revealing the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*).
This chapter consists of two parts:
first, the question; second, the answer.
Within the answer, there are three sections:
First, the manifestation of the jeweled stūpa;
second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing for the sake of the great assembly... onwards, the clarification of the causes and conditions of the jeweled stūpa;
third, from "This is called paying homage to the stūpa" onwards, a brief passage concluding the response to the preceding questions.
The first section has two parts:
first, the manifestation of the stupa and the joy of the assembly, wherein the deity questions the Buddha and the Buddha explains;
second, from "At that time the Buddha said" onwards, the manifestation of the śarīra and the praise of prostration.
Within the second major section, which clarifies dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are two parts:
first, from the beginning up to the verse, it explains the causal conditions for Śāriputra;
second, from the prose following the verse, it clarifies the causal conditions for the precious stūpa.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, the prose (gadya), and second, the verse (śloka).
Within the prose, there are two further parts:
First, the scribe’s heading;
second, from "Ānanda" onwards, the explanation of what the Tathāgata spoke.
This section contains two parts:
First, the account of his previous birth is clarified;
second, from "These three princes" onwards, the events of his present life are clarified.
Within this, there are three parts:
First, the causes and conditions for the relinquishing of the body are clarified;
second, from "At that time, the prince returned to where the tigress was" onwards, the actual relinquishing of the body is clarified;
third, from "At that time, the eldest prince" onwards, the grief and suffering of the retinue are clarified.
Regarding the first part, there are three sections:
first, the account of traveling to the mountain and deliberating together;
second, from "At that time, the princes... onwards, the account of seeing the tigress and deliberating together.
Third, from the passage beginning "At that time, the third prince," below, the contemplation of sacrificing one's body is clarified.
There are four reasons by which it is known that [the tigress] had been born for seven days:
first, there were seven spots on the forehead of each of the tiger cubs;...
Second, he saw his eyes first open;
third, when a tiger was on the verge of death from hunger, it could be known that it had not eaten for seven days;
fourth, spirits and deities spoke to him, such as when a tree spirit guided ten thousand fish—these accounts simply do not appear in the sutras.
Regarding the third section, the clarification of contemplating the relinquishment of the body, there are three parts:
first, contemplating the arrival of the time to relinquish the body;
second, from "For what reason" onwards, the actual contemplation of the desire to relinquish the body.
Third, from the section "Brave and Resolute" onwards, he dispatches his two elder brothers.
Regarding the second main point, "The Actual Intention to Renounce," there are two parts:
first, contemplating the renunciation of the body to cultivate the causes for nirvana; [and second, the actual act of renunciation].
Second, from "Furthermore, if one abandons this body" onwards, there is the contemplation of abandoning the body to seek the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
This section consists of two parts;
the first involves contemplating that this body possesses four types of impermanence (*anityatā*).
The second section, from "Today I... onwards, concerns the contemplation of cultivating the causes [of liberation].

Within this, first, the suffering [of the body] is clarified; next, from "Yet it cannot be avoided," the impermanence [of the body] is clarified; next, from "This body is not solid," its emptiness and non-self are clarified; and finally, from "It is as loathsome as a thief," its impurity is clarified.
Regarding the second section, which clarifies the causes, the first part explains one's own practice; from the words "In saṃsāra" onwards, it explains the practice of transforming others.
Within the second section, which seeks the fruit of nirvāṇa, there are two parts:
the first explains contemplating the afflictions of the body.
The second section, from "Therefore, I now" onwards, seeks the fruit of nirvāṇa.
Within this, first, it clarifies suffering and impermanence;
second, from "Only" onwards, it clarifies emptiness and non-self.
Third, from the passage "This body is impure" onwards, it clarifies impurity.
Within the second section, "Seeking Nirvana," there are two parts: first, the clarification of self-realization; [the second is the clarification of teaching others].
Second, from "Establishing it as such" onwards, the text clarifies the transformation of others.
Regarding the first [of these two], there are two parts:
first, the general seeking of nirvana; [the second follows].
From "eternally free" (*yong li*) downward, the text clarifies the separate pursuit of three points, which are threefold:
first, seeking liberation; second, from "non-" (*wu*) downward, seeking prajñā; and third, from "endowed with" (*ju zu*) downward, seeking the Dharma-body.
In the second major section, "The Actual Relinquishing of the Body," there are two parts:
first, explaining how the prince made a vow to relinquish his body and manifested various auspicious omens;
second, from the passage beginning with "At that time, the tiger... onwards, explaining how he was devoured by the tiger.
Within the third major section concerning the sorrow and suffering of the retinue, there are three parts:
first, an explanation of the sorrow and suffering of the two elder brothers;
second, from the words "The Little Prince" onwards, an explanation of the sorrow and suffering of the attendants.
Third, from the passage beginning "At that time, the queen... downwards, the text clarifies the sorrow and suffering of the parents.
Within the second major section, the verse portion, there are three parts:
the first two lines provide a general explanation of the overall intent of giving away the body;...
Second, from "I recall my past lives" onwards, the verse properly corresponds to the preceding prose;
third, from "The Buddha addressed the tree deity" onwards, five and a half verses clarify the connection between the ancient and the present.
The detailed analysis of the textual divisions need not be discussed at length here.
The "Chapter on Praising the Buddha" constitutes the third major section, clarifying the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding dedication) portion.
According to the seven-fascicle version of the sutra, this consists of two chapters:
The first chapter praises the virtues of the speaker, which constitutes the circulation through eulogy;
the final chapter clarifies the propagation of the taught Dharma, which constitutes the circulation through entrustment.
These four fascicles of the sutra consist solely of praises for its dissemination and lack a formal entrustment (*parindanā*).
They comprise two sections:
the first clarifies how bodhisattvas from other lands praise the Buddhas of those lands; the second clarifies how the great beings of this land extol the Buddha of this world.
As for the reason why each side offers praise to the other: it is because the virtues of the speakers are praised as being no different from one another.
Within the section on praising others, the initial prose passage presents the person who praises, while the subsequent verse presents the matter that is praised.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, nineteen lines of praise; second, one line of dedication.
Regarding the first part, there are three sections:
First, the seven lines praise form and sound;
second, the seven lines from "Wisdom is quiescent" downward extol merit and wisdom;
third, the five lines from "The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One" downward provide the concluding summary.
Regarding the first section, there are three parts:
the first three lines and a half praise the physical marks and signs;
the subsequent one line and a half praise the voice.

Regarding the "six kinds of purity": first, the voice of Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara; second, the voice of Great Benevolence and Gentle Melody; third, the voice of Great Brahmā’s Purity; fourth, the voice of Universal Illumination of Great Light; fifth, the voice of the Lion’s Fearlessness; and sixth, the voice of the Heroic Man among Gods and Humans.
The next two lines are the conclusion; therein, one line concludes the discussion of sound and one line concludes the discussion of form.
Within the second section praising merit and wisdom, there are two parts:
the first one and a half lines praise internal virtues;
The second section, from "For the sake of all sentient beings" down to five and a half lines, praises the virtue of external transformation (*bāhya-vinaya*).
Within the internal virtues, the first half-line praises wisdom, the next half-line praises merit, and the final half-line provides a simile.

Within the praise of external transformation (*paravivartana*), the first verse-half expresses the manifestation [of the Buddha’s activity]: the first half-line expresses the removal of suffering, and the second half-line expresses the bestowing of happiness.

The subsequent four and a half verses provide a detailed explanation; therein, the first one and a half lines clarify the essence of removing suffering and bestowing happiness, while the following three lines clarify the specific matters of removing suffering and bestowing happiness.

Within the third major section, the "Synthetic Conclusion," the first two lines clarify the immeasurability of the Buddha’s virtues; the next two lines clarify that no one can fully know them; and the final line clarifies the praise that cannot be exhausted.
The textual characteristics are evident.
Regarding the second major section, the praise by the Great Being here, there are two parts:
first, the praise by Śraddhālakṣaṇā, and second, the praise by the tree deity.
Within the section on praising the characteristics of faith, there are two parts:
first, ten and a half lines of specific praise;
second, from "The Tathāgata knows all" onwards, six and a half lines of general eulogy.
Regarding the first [section], there are three parts:
first, eight lines praising the physical body (*rūpakāya*); second, one and a half lines praising merit and wisdom; and third, one line as a conclusion.
Regarding the first [of these three], there are two parts:
The first four lines praise the physical body;
from "Radiance" onwards, they praise the functions of the physical body.
The second section praises the visible aspects of merit and wisdom.
In the third summary, the first half concludes the description of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), while the second half concludes that of merit and wisdom.
Within the third major section, the general praise, the first two lines praise merit and wisdom, and the subsequent four and a half lines praise the form-body.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, practicing external transformation; second, practicing internal virtue.
Regarding the latter [section], there are likewise two parts:
The first two lines describe external transformation, while the subsequent two and a half lines describe internal virtue;
the textual structure is clear.
In the second section, the tree spirit’s praise, the initial portion identifies the person offering the praise, while from "Namo" (*namas*) downward, it sets forth the matters being extolled.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, twenty-five and a half lines consisting of the tree deity’s praise; second, two lines consisting of the Tathāgata’s response.
Regarding the first part, there are three sections:
The first nineteen and a half lines collectively praise the two bodies of response and transformation;
the second, from "the body of a śrāvaka" downward for five lines, separately praises the dharma-body;
the third, from "I now have no doubt" downward for one line, concludes the request.
Regarding the first section, there are two parts:
the first twelve and a half lines are a formal eulogy;
the second, from "I constantly think of the Buddha" downward, consists of seven lines that clarify yearning and aspiration.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
the first four and a half lines praise the essence of the three bodies;
the second, from "The Buddha appears in the world" downward, consists of eight lines praising the function.
The first two [sections] consist of two and a half verses praising wisdom, followed by two verses praising merit.
Within the first of these, there are two [parts]:
The first line expresses praise, while the subsequent one and a half lines provide an explanation.
"Non-Dharma" refers to false teachings;
"non-path" refers to false paths.
"Knowing existence" refers to knowing the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Non-existence" refers to knowing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Knowing that the fundamental nature is pure is knowing the single reality-truth (*eka-tattva-satya*).
The second section, the praise of its function, has two parts:
first, one line that generally expresses the rarity of transcending the world; second, seven lines that clarify these rare events.
Within this, there are two further divisions:
The first two lines praise the virtue of outward transformation;
the subsequent five lines, beginning with "Excellent," praise the virtue of inward realization.
Within this section, there are two parts:
The first two lines clarify the wisdom capable of realization;
the three lines from "all" (*sarva*) downward clarify the principle realized.

Regarding "the tranquility of the faculties" (*indriya-śānti*): it means that afflictions do not arise within the faculties; this is the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"The Great City of Excellent Tranquility" refers to the Great Nirvana, which is the unconditioned state of the extinction of qualities.
"Profound Samādhi" refers to meditative concentration (dhyāna).
"Entering the sphere of activity of all Buddhas" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).
This meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom constitute the virtue of bodhi.

Within the second section concerning the realized principle, the first verse clarifies the emptiness of the noble path, the next verse clarifies the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharma*), and the final verse clarifies the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva*).
"Body is entirely empty and quiescent" means that the path of the Two Vehicles is empty.
"Conduct is void and also empty" means that the Mahāyāna path is the sphere of practice of the Tathāgata; this path is empty, and even that emptiness is empty.
Regarding the phrase "the nature and characteristics are also empty": it means that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is empty because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is without characteristics (*animitta*), its characteristics are also empty.
In the second major section, which clarifies longing and yearning, there are two parts:
first, the four lines clarify that longing and the wish to see [the Buddha];
second, from "I only pray" onwards, it expresses the prayer for the Buddha’s compassionate acceptance.

Regarding the beginning and middle [of the section], the first line cites the merit of recollecting the Buddha to express the aspiration to see him; the next line cites the merit of prostrating to express the aspiration to see him; the next line cites the cultivation of compassionate conduct to express the aspiration to see him; and the final line cites the fire of longing and anxiety to express the aspiration to see him.

Regarding the second vow, which concerns the Buddha’s acceptance, the first line of the verse aspires that the water of the Dharma may extinguish the fire of sorrow; the next line of verse aspires that the Buddha may manifest his body so that I may see him constantly; and the final line of verse serves as the concluding request.
The second major section, the specific praise of the Dharma-body, contains two parts:
the first three lines praise the profound wisdom of the Dharma-body;
the second part, from "The sphere of the Tathāgata’s activity" onwards in two lines, clarifies that sentient beings cannot know it.
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, one and a half lines clarify the falsity of birth and death;
second, from "The Tathāgata" onwards, one and a half lines clarify the reality of the Dharmakāya.

"Pure as lapis lazuli" means that the essence of the Dharmakāya is free from all manifold characteristics; therefore, it is called "pure," which refers to the principle of the threefold absence of self-nature (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Regarding the third section on the conclusion, the first half concludes that the Dharma [Body] should consist of two bodies:
"Buddha" refers to the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya),
and "the sphere of activity" refers to the Dharma Body (dharmakāya).
The second half requests the manifestation of the transformation body.

*Commentary on the Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, one fascicle. Postscript to the Carved Edition of the *Commentary on the Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. The aforementioned *Commentary on the Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* in one fascicle was composed by the Great Master Jiaxiang of the Sui dynasty based upon the four-fascicle sūtra text translated by Dharmakṣema.
The phrasing is concise while the meaning is manifest, and the structural divisions are particularly refined; it will be of great benefit to students.
Recently, someone brought a copy here and planned to have it carved into printing blocks to broaden its circulation.
Alas! Although this text was transmitted to our land in ancient times, it remained obscure for a very long period.
That it has become manifest now is perhaps due to destiny.

Regretting that there were not a few errors resulting from the transcription of characters such as "lu" for "yu" or omissions and deletions, I have sought out the original manuscript and performed a meticulous collation; I have added marginal annotations and transmitted this to the students of the printing house.
I have briefly inscribed this at the end of the scroll to mark the date and year.
Written with reverence by the Śramaṇa Junsei of Mount Hiei at Honnō-in on the East Creek.
